arXiv:2605.12947v1 [stat.ML] 13 May 2026

When Should an AI Workflow Release?
Always-Valid Inference for Black-Box Generate-Verify Systems

Young Hyun Cho ††thanks: Department of Statistics, Purdue University. Email: cho472@purdue.edu.    Will Wei Sun ††thanks: Mitch Daniels School of Business, Purdue University. Email: sun244@purdue.edu. Corresponding author.
Abstract

LLM-enabled AI workflows increasingly produce outputs through iterative generate-evaluate-revise loops. Each iteration can improve the candidate, but it also creates a release decision: when to stop and output the current result? This raises a statistical challenge because deployment-time evaluator scores are adaptively generated and repeatedly monitored, yet the likelihood models or exchangeability assumptions typically used for calibration are unavailable. We propose an always-valid release wrapper for existing generator-evaluator pipelines. The wrapper builds a hard-negative reference pool of high-scoring failures, calibrates deployment-time evaluator scores against this pool, and accumulates the resulting evidence with an e-process. This separates two roles: the reference pool turns black-box scores into conservative evidence, while the e-process provides validity under optional stopping. In theory, we show that a conservative reference pool yields finite-sample control of the probability of releasing on infeasible tasks, that is, tasks for which the given workflow is not capable of producing a reliable solution. We also characterize conditions under which the same conservative rule still achieves nontrivial release on feasible tasks. In an MBPP+ coding-agent case study, the wrapper reduces premature incorrect release relative to baseline stopping rules while still releasing on tasks for which the workflow repeatedly accumulates moderate supporting evidence.

Keywords: Agentic AI workflows; e-process; large language models; selective release; sequential hypothesis testing.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as components of AI workflows rather than as one-shot predictors. In these workflows, a model is called repeatedly, candidate outputs are evaluated or revised over multiple rounds, and later calls are conditioned on what has already happened in the interaction. Industry reports describe growing interest in AI systems that move beyond chat-style assistance toward more workflow-integrated forms of problem solving (McKinsey & Company 2025, McKinsey & Company 2026). Guidance from AI labs likewise emphasizes traces, task outcomes, and failure modes as central objects to monitor in multi-step AI systems (OpenAI 2026, Anthropic 2026a). These developments broaden the scope of statistical decision-making for AI systems, bringing into view the interaction trajectory itself and the stopping decision that determines whether an output is released.

A recurring structure is an adaptive generate-evaluate-revise loop. At step tt, the system produces a candidate output and observes an imperfect signal about its quality. This signal may come from tests, checkers, execution feedback, or learned judges; its role is not to certify correctness, but to provide evidence that the workflow may use when deciding whether to continue or release. Additional rounds can improve the candidate, but they also consume tokens, latency, and compute, and practical coding-agent systems already track these costs and activity patterns (Anthropic 2026b, Anthropic 2026c). Thus the deployment problem is a stopping problem: the system must decide when the evidence accumulated along an adaptive trajectory is strong enough to justify releasing the current output.

Figure 1 abstracts a general generate-evaluate-revise workflow. This structure appears across mathematical reasoning with learned or process-level verifiers, coding workflows with execution feedback, and tool-using, web, robotic, or embodied agents that revise actions from external feedback (Cobbe et al. 2021, Lightman et al. 2023, Wang et al. 2024, Setlur et al. 2024, Shao et al. 2024, Guo et al. 2025, Ma et al. 2025, Hutter and Pradel 2026, Yao et al. 2022, Schick et al. 2023, Ahn et al. 2022, Wang et al. 2023, Zhou et al. 2024). Across these domains, intermediate evaluator signals are useful but imperfect, so the release decision observes a black-box evidence stream rather than a certificate of correctness.

This adaptivity creates a statistical stopping problem. If a workflow repeatedly generates and evaluates candidates, then an incorrect or unreliable candidate receives repeated opportunities to obtain a favorable evaluator signal. A rule that simply waits for a high score can therefore be misled by repeated monitoring. This is the workflow analogue of pp-hacking, where repeated looks at noisy evidence can inflate false discoveries unless the stopping rule is accounted for (Ramdas and Wang 2025). The relevant statistical question is therefore not whether a candidate has a large raw score at a single step, but whether the evidence accumulated along the adaptive trajectory is strong enough to support release.

We treat this as a black-box release problem for adaptive workflows. The wrapper does not retrain the generator or evaluator, nor model the distribution of workflow traces. It adds a distribution-free decision layer using verifier signals observed during deployment. The goal is to control false release on instances where the given pipeline cannot produce a reliable solution, while still allowing release when repeated evidence supports feasibility.

Figure 2 shows the decision layer proposed in this paper. The hard-negative reference pool supplies a failure-side calibration anchor: a deployment-time score is not judged by its raw magnitude, but by how extreme it is relative to scores previously achieved by high-scoring failures. This converts heterogeneous black-box evaluator signals into calibrated stepwise pp-values. An e-process then accumulates these calibrated values over time and releases only after the accumulated evidence crosses an anytime-valid threshold.

1.1 Our Contributions

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

Statistical formulation of safe release in adaptive workflow. We formulate verifier-guided adaptive workflows as a selective release problem, with safety measured by ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=0)\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=0), the probability of release on instances for which the specified generator-verifier pipeline is not capable of producing a reliable solution. This casts deployment-time stopping as a statistical control problem rather than a heuristic rule for black-box verifier scores.

Methodology. We introduce a modular wrapper for black-box generator-evaluator workflows. The wrapper does not retrain either component or model the distribution of workflow traces. It builds a conservative hard-negative reference pool from offline failures, calibrates deployment-time verifier scores by upper-tail ranks against this pool, and accumulates the calibrated evidence through an e-process. This modular design is useful for rapidly changing AI systems because updates to the generator, evaluator, or task distribution can be handled by rebuilding the reference pool, while the release rule remains unchanged.

Theory. The main theoretical issue is how to construct valid sequential testing from adaptive black-box verifier scores. Likelihood-ratio e-processes require conditional score laws, while conformal rank arguments require exchangeability; neither structure is naturally available in our problem. We introduce a failure-side calibration dominance condition under which empirical upper-tail ranks become conditionally super-uniform pp-values despite history-dependent score generation. Combined with pp-to-e accumulation, this yields ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=0)≤α\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=0)\leq\alpha. We also give a finite-horizon result showing that our wrapper can release on feasible tasks when correct candidates provide enough calibrated evidence over time.

Empirics. We use MBPP+ code generation (Liu et al. 2023) as a coding-agent instance of the broader release problem. The case study shows that baseline stopping rules based on confidence or score stability can release too early, while one-step calibrated thresholding can become too conservative when no single verifier score is decisive. In contrast, the proposed wrapper accumulates moderate evidence across iterations, reducing premature incorrect release while still releasing on many tasks that the underlying workflow eventually solves.

1.2 Related Work

Recent work across LLM-enabled workflows increasingly relies on iterative generation with external or learned feedback. In mathematical reasoning, trained verifiers, process reward models, and test-time search guide candidate solutions (Cobbe et al. 2021, Lightman et al. 2023, Setlur et al. 2024, Wang et al. 2024, Shao et al. 2024, Guo et al. 2025). In software and agentic settings, execution results, tool outputs, browser states, or environment feedback play a similar role in guiding revision (Ma et al. 2025, Hutter and Pradel 2026, Yao et al. 2022, Schick et al. 2023, Madaan et al. 2023, Shinn et al. 2023, Ahn et al. 2022, Wang et al. 2023, Zhou et al. 2024). When deployment-time stopping is addressed, it is often handled by heuristics based on confidence, entropy, stability, or related proxies for sufficient progress (Li et al. 2024, Wu et al. 2025a, Mao et al. 2025, Laaouach 2025, Quamar and Areeb 2025, Wu et al. 2025b, Huang et al. 2026). By contrast, we treat release as a statistical control problem for a black-box workflow and develop a wrapper that can be layered on top of an existing pipeline without retraining either component. Our setting is also related to Xie et al. (2026), which develops stopping rules from signals from internal reasoning traces. The distinction is that their approach relies on white-box access to internal markers of the reasoning process, whereas we assume no access to internal states and operate only through external verifier scores.

Methodologically, our work connects to always-valid inference and e-processes (Ramdas and Wang 2025, Su et al. 2026), which provide time-uniform validity once a valid stream of stepwise evidence is available. In our problem, however, the main difficulty arises earlier: the deployment-time verifier scores are adaptive, heterogeneous, and generated by a black-box workflow, so they are not themselves valid e-values or pp-values. Our contribution is therefore not the use of e-processes alone, but the construction of a valid testing interface for these scores. Moreover, our rank-calibration step is related to conformal prediction (Vovk et al. 2005, Barber et al. 2023), because both approaches compare a new score with a reference collection. The source of validity, however, is different. Standard conformal guarantees rely on exchangeability between the calibration sample and the new observation, whereas the adaptive score process generated by a black-box evaluator–optimizer loop generally admits neither exchangeability nor a tractable likelihood model. We address this by constructing a pool of hard-negative failures that serves as a conservative failure-side anchor. Under a one-sided dominance condition, this reference pool yields stepwise-valid pp-values, which can then be accumulated through the e-process to obtain always-valid release decisions.

2 Problem Setup and Preliminaries

We study a sequential release problem for an input instance x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, drawn from a task distribution PXP_{X}. The input may be a programming task, a mathematical problem, or another task handled by an adaptive AI workflow. A generator produces a sequence of candidate outputs, and after each candidate an evaluator or verifier returns a scalar score summarizing current evidence for correctness. The wrapper observes this evolving interaction and must decide whether to release the current candidate or continue searching.

Formally, at each step t≥1t\geq 1, the generator proposes a candidate output CtC_{t}, and the verifier returns a scalar signal St∈𝒮⊆ℝS_{t}\in\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathbb{R}. Let

Ht:=(x,C1,S1,…,Ct,St)H_{t}:=(x,C_{1},S_{1},\ldots,C_{t},S_{t})

denote the observable interaction history up to step tt, and let 𝒢t:=σ⁡(Ht)\mathcal{G}_{t}:=\sigma(H_{t}) be the corresponding filtration. The wrapper uses HtH_{t} to decide whether to release the current candidate. Let Dt∈{0,1}D_{t}\in\{0,1\} be the step-tt decision, where Dt=1D_{t}=1 means release now and Dt=0D_{t}=0 means continue. We require DtD_{t} to be 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t}-measurable. The release time is

τ:=inf{t≥1:Dt=1},\tau:=\inf\{t\geq 1:D_{t}=1\},

with the convention τ=∞\tau=\infty if the wrapper never releases. Given a maximum horizon TmaxT_{\max}, the system releases CτC_{\tau} if τ≤Tmax\tau\leq T_{\max} and abstains otherwise. We write

D:=𝟏{τ≤Tmax}D:=\mathbf{1}\{\tau\leq T_{\max}\}

for the terminal release indicator.

Let Yt∈{0,1}Y_{t}\in\{0,1\} denote whether candidate CtC_{t} is truly correct. Thus YtY_{t} is a task-specific correctness label: in coding, Yt=1Y_{t}=1 may mean that the generated program passes the full hidden test suite; in math reasoning, Yt=1Y_{t}=1 may mean that the final answer is mathematically correct. The wrapper does not observe YtY_{t} online; it observes only the verifier score StS_{t}, which may be informative but imperfect.

We also introduce a latent feasibility state

F∈{0,1}.F\in\{0,1\}.

The variable FF distinguishes two qualitatively different reasons that a candidate may be incorrect. A candidate may be wrong simply because the search is still ongoing, even though the underlying generator-verifier pipeline is capable of eventually producing a reliable solution. Alternatively, the instance may be effectively beyond the capability of the given pipeline, so that even high verifier scores do not correspond to genuine eventual success. We interpret F=1F=1 as the feasible regime and F=0F=0 as the infeasible regime. Importantly, FF is a property of the entire pipeline applied to the instance, not of the instance alone.

This distinction is useful in adaptive workflows. In coding, an incorrect program may still pass many visible tests, so a high StS_{t} can reflect overfitting rather than true correctness. In mathematical reasoning, an incorrect derivation may appear polished and receive a favorable judge score even though the problem is beyond the model’s effective capability. The wrapper should not be penalized for early incorrect candidates on feasible tasks, but it should control the probability of release on infeasible tasks.

Example 1 (Coding and math reasoning).
  • •

    Coding. xx is a programming problem, CtC_{t} is a proposed program, and StS_{t} may be the fraction of visible unit tests passed. The label Yt=1Y_{t}=1 means that the program is actually correct, for example because it passes the full hidden test suite. The state F=1F=1 means that the specified generator-verifier pipeline can in principle produce a reliable solution for this task; F=0F=0 means that it cannot, even though some intermediate programs may achieve deceptively high verifier scores.

  • •

    Math reasoning. xx is a mathematical problem, CtC_{t} is a reasoning trace together with a final answer, and StS_{t} may come from exact answer matching, symbolic checking, or an LLM judge. The label Yt=1Y_{t}=1 means that the final answer is mathematically correct. The state F=1F=1 means that the pipeline can in principle reach a reliable solution for this problem; F=0F=0 means that it cannot, even if some candidate derivations appear plausible or receive high verifier scores.

The release decision can be viewed through the lens of hypothesis testing. The infeasible regime F=0F=0 plays the role of a null state, while the feasible regime F=1F=1 plays the role of an alternative state. Releasing a candidate, that is, deciding D=1D=1, is then analogous to rejecting the null. This perspective leads to two primitive criteria. The first is the false-release probability on infeasible instances,

ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=0),\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=0), (1)

which measures how often the wrapper is misled into release when the pipeline is not capable of producing a reliable solution. This quantity plays the role of a Type I error analogue.

The second is the release probability on feasible instances,

ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=1),\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=1), (2)

which measures how often the wrapper releases when a reliable solution is attainable. This quantity plays the role of power. A wrapper that always abstains would trivially drive (1) to zero, but only at the cost of also setting ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=1)=0\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=1)=0.

Accordingly, our main safety target is

ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=0)≤α,\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=0)\leq\alpha, (3)

which is the analogue of Type I error control at level α\alpha.

The most user-facing notion of reliability is the release-conditional failure rate

Rout:=ℙ⁡(Yτ=0∣D=1),R_{\mathrm{out}}:=\mathbb{P}(Y_{\tau}=0\mid D=1), (4)

which is the probability that a released candidate is incorrect. This is the ultimate practical target, but it is difficult to control directly because the released candidate is selected through a history-dependent stopping rule and the wrapper observes only verifier scores rather than ground-truth correctness. For this reason, our theory focuses first on the more tractable target (3), together with the companion feasible-side release probability (2).

The next proposition links the primitive safety target to the release-conditional failure rate.

Proposition 1.

Let π0=ℙ⁡(F=0)\pi_{0}=\mathbb{P}(F=0). Suppose the wrapper satisfies ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=0)≤α\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=0)\leq\alpha. Then

Rout≤ℙ⁡(Yτ=0∣D=1,F=1)+(1−ℙ⁡(Yτ=0∣D=1,F=1))​π0​απ0​α+(1−π0)​ℙ​(D=1∣F=1).\begin{split}R_{\mathrm{out}}&\leq\mathbb{P}(Y_{\tau}=0\mid D=1,F=1)\\ &\quad+\Bigl(1-\mathbb{P}(Y_{\tau}=0\mid D=1,F=1)\Bigr)\frac{\pi_{0}\alpha}{\pi_{0}\alpha+(1-\pi_{0})\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=1)}.\end{split} (5)

The decomposition in (5) highlights the division of roles between the underlying reasoning pipeline and the release wrapper. The first term reflects performance on feasible instances and is determined by the quality of the base generator once the wrapper releases. The second term isolates the contribution from infeasible instances and is controlled directly through the false-release bound α\alpha.

The primitive safety target (3) requires tools from sequential inference. A natural baseline is to compute, at each step tt, a significance measure based on the current verifier signal, for example, a pp-value that would be valid if the analysis stopped at time tt alone, and to release as soon as this quantity falls below a nominal threshold. While intuitive, this strategy is fundamentally unreliable under repeated monitoring.

Proposition 2 (Failure of naive stopping).

Fix α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and let (pt)t≥1(p_{t})_{t\geq 1} be a sequence of [0,1][0,1]-valued statistics adapted to a filtration (𝒢t)t≥1(\mathcal{G}_{t})_{t\geq 1}. Define τnaive:=inf{t≥1:pt≤α}.\tau_{\mathrm{naive}}:=\inf\{t\geq 1:p_{t}\leq\alpha\}. If there exists a deterministic sequence (ct)t≥1⊂[0,1](c_{t})_{t\geq 1}\subset[0,1] such that for all t≥1t\geq 1, ℙ⁡(pt≤α∣𝒢t−1,F=0)≥ct\mathbb{P}(p_{t}\leq\alpha\mid\mathcal{G}_{t-1},F=0)\geq c_{t} almost surely, then for any T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N},

ℙ(τnaive≤T∣F=0)≥1−exp(−∑t=1Tct).\mathbb{P}(\tau_{\mathrm{naive}}\leq T\mid F=0)\geq 1-\exp\!\left(-\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}\right).

Consequently, if ∑t≥1ct=∞\sum_{t\geq 1}c_{t}=\infty, then ℙ⁡(τnaive<∞∣F=0)=1.\mathbb{P}(\tau_{\mathrm{naive}}<\infty\mid F=0)=1.

Proposition 2 shows that repeated thresholding of stepwise significance measures does not yield sequential safety. Even if each individual step has only a tiny chance of producing a misleadingly favorable statistic, repeated monitoring causes these risks to accumulate over time. In our setting, this is the sequential analogue of “pp-hacking”.

To avoid this failure, we need a notion of evidence that remains valid under arbitrary stopping times. E-processes provide exactly this type of time-uniform control.

Definition 1 (e-process).

Fix a null hypothesis H0H_{0}. Let (ℋt)t≥0(\mathcal{H}_{t})_{t\geq 0} be a filtration. A nonnegative (ℋt)(\mathcal{H}_{t})-adapted process (Et)t≥0(E_{t})_{t\geq 0} is an e-process for H0H_{0} if E0=1E_{0}=1 and, under H0H_{0},

𝔼H0​[Et∣ℋt−1]≤Et−1almost surely for all ​t≥1.\mathbb{E}_{H_{0}}[E_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}]\leq E_{t-1}\qquad\text{almost surely for all }t\geq 1. (6)

In our application, the null hypothesis corresponds to the infeasible regime F=0F=0. The following classical inequality makes the time-uniform validity of an e-process precise.

Lemma 1 (Ville’s inequality (Doob 1939)).

If (Et)t≥0(E_{t})_{t\geq 0} is an e-process for H0H_{0}, then

ℙH0​(supt≥1Et≥1α)≤α,\mathbb{P}_{H_{0}}\!\left(\sup_{t\geq 1}E_{t}\geq\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)\leq\alpha,

for any α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1). Equivalently, for τα:=inf{t≥1:Et≥1α},\tau_{\alpha}:=\inf\left\{t\geq 1:E_{t}\geq\frac{1}{\alpha}\right\}, we have ℙH0​(τα<∞)≤α.\mathbb{P}_{H_{0}}(\tau_{\alpha}<\infty)\leq\alpha.

Lemma 1 implies that constructing an e-process is sufficient for always-valid safe release. In classical sequential testing, e-processes are often derived from likelihood ratios (Ramdas et al. 2023). Our setting, however, is black-box and likelihood-free: the verifier scores are heterogeneous, adaptively generated, and need not admit a tractable parametric model. A robust alternative is p-to-e calibration (Vovk and Wang 2021), which transforms a sequence of valid pp-values into an e-process. The main challenge, therefore, is to construct valid pp-values from the raw verifier scores StS_{t}.

3 Proposed Method and Its Statistical Properties

In this section, we construct the failure-calibrated release wrapper and explain how it provides a statistical testing interface for black-box verifier scores.

3.1 Algorithm overview

At each interaction step tt, the system produces a candidate output CtC_{t} and a verifier score StS_{t}. The wrapper proceeds in three stages.

  1. 1.

    Offline hard-negative reference-pool construction. Using an auxiliary calibration collection, construct a pool ℛ\mathcal{R} of incorrect candidates that nevertheless receive unusually favorable verifier scores.

  2. 2.

    Reference-pool calibration. Compare the current score StS_{t} to the fixed pool ℛ\mathcal{R} and convert it into an empirical upper-tail pp-value ptp_{t}.

  3. 3.

    Sequential evidence accumulation and release. Transform the calibrated pp-values into e-values, accumulate them over time, and release only when the resulting evidence process crosses 1/α1/\alpha.

The wrapper acts on rank-calibrated evidence rather than on raw verifier scores. A score that appears large in isolation may not be compelling if similar scores are frequently produced by incorrect outputs. A score that remains extreme even relative to a pool of hard negatives is more meaningful evidence against the infeasible regime.

3.2 Offline hard-negative reference-pool construction

The first step is to construct a conservative reference pool ℛ={R1,…,Rn}\mathcal{R}=\{R_{1},\ldots,R_{n}\}, which will later be used to calibrate online verifier scores. The need for such a pool comes from the fact that the raw score StS_{t} is often heterogeneous across tasks and difficult to interpret on an absolute scale. In code generation, for example, a score of 0.8 may mean that the candidate passes 80% of a visible test suite, but whether that is impressive depends on the task and on how easy the visible tests are to overfit. In mathematical reasoning, a high judge score may simply reflect that a derivation looks plausible even if it is incorrect. We therefore build the reference pool from hard negatives, namely incorrect candidates that nevertheless receive favorable verifier scores, and evaluate each online score through its relative extremeness against this benchmark.

Formally, let 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}} denote a calibration set drawn from the same task family. For each x∈𝒟calx\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}, we generate candidate output CC, compute its online verifier score s=𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(x,C)s=\mathsf{Ver}(x,C), and then apply a stronger offline adjudicator 𝒜⁡(x,C)∈{0,1}\mathcal{A}(x,C)\in\{0,1\}, where 𝒜⁡(x,C)=1\mathcal{A}(x,C)=1 means that the candidate is judged correct by the stronger offline criterion. We retain only those candidates with 𝒜⁡(x,C)=0\mathcal{A}(x,C)=0.

Among the incorrect candidates, we retain only those whose scores lie in the upper tail of the failure distribution. This restriction is important because a pool built from arbitrary failures need not be conservative for selective release. If many reference scores come from obviously poor candidates with very low verifier values, then even a moderately favorable online score may appear artificially extreme, producing anti-conservative calibrated pp-values. Hard-negative selection instead enlarges the right tail of the failure-side reference distribution, focusing calibration on the score region most relevant to false release.

To make this selection explicit, let {Γq:q∈(0,1]}\{\Gamma_{q}:q\in(0,1]\} be a family of upper-tail selection rules, where Γq\Gamma_{q} retains the upper 100​q%100q\% of incorrect-candidate scores. In the MBPP+ case study, Γq\Gamma_{q} is applied to visible verifier scores among incorrect bank-split candidates. In particular, Γ0.55\Gamma_{0.55} yields the top55 pool used in the main analysis of the experiments.

After constructing a candidate pool, we compute the induced empirical upper-tail pp-values on held-out incorrect examples and examine their empirical CDF

F^​(u):=ℙ^​(pt≤u),u∈[0,1].\widehat{F}(u):=\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(p_{t}\leq u),\qquad u\in[0,1].

A conservative pool should yield an empirical CDF lying at or below the diagonal u↦uu\mapsto u. This diagnostic provides a practical screen for ruling out visibly anti-conservative candidate pools before deployment.

3.3 Reference-pool calibration and e-process construction

With the offline hard-negative pool ℛ\mathcal{R} fixed, we now construct the testing used during deployment. Let (𝒢t)t≥0(\mathcal{G}_{t})_{t\geq 0} denote the observable filtration generated by the online interaction, and define 𝒢~t:=𝒢t∨σ⁡(ℛ)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t}:=\mathcal{G}_{t}\vee\sigma(\mathcal{R}), which additionally reveals the realized reference pool.

The main obstacle is not optional stopping itself. Once a valid evidence stream is available, e-processes provide a standard mechanism for accumulating it under arbitrary stopping. The obstacle is constructing that stream from raw verifier scores. The online verifier score StS_{t} is produced by an adaptive black-box interaction, so its conditional law is history-dependent and typically unavailable. As a result, standard likelihood-based or exchangeability-based calibration cannot be applied directly. Specifically, a likelihood-ratio route would require conditional score laws under the feasible and infeasible regimes. If such laws were available, say q1,t(⋅∣𝒢t−1)q_{1,t}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{G}_{t-1}) and q0,t(⋅∣𝒢t−1)q_{0,t}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{G}_{t-1}), one could form the likelihood-ratio evidence process EtLR:=∏j=1tq1,j​(Sj∣𝒢j−1)/q0,j​(Sj∣𝒢j−1)E_{t}^{\mathrm{LR}}:=\prod_{j=1}^{t}q_{1,j}(S_{j}\mid\mathcal{G}_{j-1})/q_{0,j}(S_{j}\mid\mathcal{G}_{j-1}). In our problem, these conditional laws are not specified. The generator-verifier interaction is black-box, and the candidate CtC_{t} is adapted to the previous history. Thus neither q0,tq_{0,t} nor q1,tq_{1,t} is available as an input to the release rule.

A conformal perspective is useful because our calibration step also compares an online score with a reference collection. If R1,…,RnR_{1},\ldots,R_{n} and StS_{t} were exchangeable under the infeasible regime, the usual rank argument would yield a valid pp-value by symmetry. The key difference is the source of validity. In an adaptive generator-verifier loop, the candidate CtC_{t} is produced after observing the previous interaction, so the conditional law of StS_{t} may change with 𝒢t−1\mathcal{G}_{t-1}. Thus the online score stream is not exchangeable with a fixed offline calibration sample. The hard-negative pool is therefore not used as an exchangeable conformal calibration set. It is used as a conservative failure-side anchor, and validity will come from the following one-sided dominance condition defined in (7) rather than from exchangeability.

Assumption 1 (Failure-side calibration dominance).

Under the infeasible regime F=0F=0, the reference pool stochastically dominates the online score generation. Specifically, for every step t≥1t\geq 1 and threshold s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R},

ℙ(St≥s|𝒢~t−1,F=0)≤ℙ(S~≥s|σ(ℛ)),\mathbb{P}\!\left(S_{t}\geq s\,\middle|\,\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=0\right)\leq\mathbb{P}\!\left(\tilde{S}\geq s\,\middle|\,\sigma(\mathcal{R})\right), (7)

almost surely, where S~\tilde{S} is an independent draw from the empirical distribution supported on ℛ\mathcal{R}, conditional on σ⁡(ℛ)\sigma(\mathcal{R}).

Assumption 1 is the calibration interface between black-box LLM scores and sequential testing. It does not model the full conditional law of StS_{t}, nor does it assume that online and offline scores are exchangeable. It only requires that, under F=0F=0, the online upper tail is no heavier than the upper tail represented by the hard-negative pool. Algorithm 1 is designed to make this condition plausible by using the same generator-verifier pipeline as deployment, filtering with a stronger offline adjudicator, and retaining high-scoring failures.

Given ℛ\mathcal{R}, define the empirical upper-tail pp-value

pt:=1+∑i=1n𝟏{Ri≥St}n+1.p_{t}:=\frac{1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{R_{i}\geq S_{t}\}}{n+1}. (8)

Thus ptp_{t} is small when the current online score StS_{t} is large relative to the hard-negative benchmark. The floor 1/(n+1)1/(n+1) prevents zero pp-values when StS_{t} exceeds all reference scores.

Theorem 1 (Stepwise validity under a conservative reference pool).

Under Assumption 1, for every u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1] and every t≥1t\geq 1, it holds almost surely that

ℙ(pt≤u|𝒢~t−1,F=0)≤u.\mathbb{P}\!\left(p_{t}\leq u\,\middle|\,\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=0\right)\leq u. (9)

Theorem 1 is the point at which a raw adaptive verifier score becomes a testing object. Before Theorem 1, StS_{t} is only a black-box score whose scale and distribution are task-dependent and history-dependent. After Theorem 1, the rank-calibrated quantity ptp_{t} is conditionally super-uniform under infeasibility and can therefore be used as valid sequential testing input. This is the main technical role of the hard-negative reference pool.

The result also clarifies the respective roles of the two components of the wrapper. The hard-negative calibration step supplies validity for the transformation St↦ptS_{t}\mapsto p_{t}, while the e-process supplies optional-stopping validity for the transformation pt↦Etp_{t}\mapsto E_{t}. The contribution is the construction of an interface for adaptive black-box verifier scores, which then allows standard anytime-valid accumulation to be used.

We next convert the calibrated pp-values into an e-process. This step is standard once Theorem 1 has supplied the valid input stream. Let ft:[0,1]→[0,∞)f_{t}:[0,1]\to[0,\infty) be a predictable non-increasing betting function satisfying ∫01ft​(u)​𝑑u≤1\int_{0}^{1}f_{t}(u)\,du\leq 1 almost surely for each tt. Define

Et:=∏s=1tfs​(ps),E0:=1.E_{t}:=\prod_{s=1}^{t}f_{s}(p_{s}),\qquad E_{0}:=1.
Proposition 3 (E-process from calibrated pp-values).

Suppose (pt)t≥1(p_{t})_{t\geq 1} satisfies (9). Let (ft)t≥1(f_{t})_{t\geq 1} be a sequence of predictable non-increasing functions with ∫01ft​(u)​𝑑u≤1\int_{0}^{1}f_{t}(u)\,du\leq 1 almost surely. Then, under F=0F=0, it holds almost surely for all t≥1t\geq 1 that

𝔼[Et∣𝒢~t−1,F=0]≤Et−1.\mathbb{E}\!\left[E_{t}\mid\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=0\right]\leq E_{t-1}.

Hence (Et)t≥0(E_{t})_{t\geq 0} is an e-process for the infeasible regime.

Proposition 3 is the optional-stopping component of the wrapper. Its role is to accumulate the conditionally valid pp-values supplied by Theorem 1.

In the implementation, we use the standard truncated power-betting family (Vovk and Wang 2021, Grünwald et al. 2020). Specifically, for η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1) and truncation level M≥1M\geq 1, let f(η,M)​(u):=c​min⁡(u−η,M)f^{(\eta,M)}(u):=c\min(u^{-\eta},M), where cc is chosen so that ∫01f(η,M)​(u)​𝑑u=1\int_{0}^{1}f^{(\eta,M)}(u)\,du=1.

We define the release time and terminal release indicator by

τα:=inf{t≥1:Et≥1/α},D:=𝟏{τα≤Tmax}.\tau_{\alpha}:=\inf\{t\geq 1:E_{t}\geq 1/\alpha\},\qquad D:=\mathbf{1}\{\tau_{\alpha}\leq T_{\max}\}.

That is, the wrapper releases only when the accumulated evidence against the infeasible regime exceeds 1/α1/\alpha within the maximum horizon TmaxT_{\max}. Otherwise, it abstains. The detailed always-valid release wrapper procedure is included in Algorithm 2.

Proposition 4 (Always-valid false-release control).

Let DD be defined as above from an e-process (Et)t≥0(E_{t})_{t\geq 0} satisfying Proposition 3. Then

ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=0)≤α.\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=0)\leq\alpha.

Proposition 4 is the primitive safety guarantee delivered by the wrapper. Combined with Proposition 1, it explains why conservative false-release control on infeasible instances yields meaningful protection for the release-conditional risk of the deployed system.

3.4 Feasible-side release

The false-release guarantee in Proposition 4 controls the Type I side of the release problem. A useful wrapper must also remain active on feasible instances. If safety alone were the objective, the trivial rule that always abstains would satisfy Proposition 4, but it would have no deployment value because it sets the feasible-side release probability to zero. We therefore complement the safety result with an analysis of when the proposed wrapper releases under F=1F=1.

The feasible-side analysis cannot be assumption-free. When feasible and infeasible transcripts are indistinguishable to the wrapper, no black-box rule can release frequently under F=1F=1 while controlling release under F=0F=0. Proposition 5 formalizes this limitation.

Proposition 5 (Observable-separation limit for feasible-side release).

Fix a horizon TT. Let PfT=ℒ⁡((ℛ,HT)∣F=f)P_{f}^{T}=\mathcal{L}((\mathcal{R},H_{T})\mid F=f), f∈{0,1}f\in\{0,1\}, be the conditional law of the observed transcript available to the release rule by time TT. Then any terminal release rule DT∈{0,1}D_{T}\in\{0,1\} that is measurable with respect to σ⁡(ℛ,HT)\sigma(\mathcal{R},H_{T}) satisfies

ℙ⁡(DT=1∣F=1)≤ℙ⁡(DT=1∣F=0)+TV⁡(P1T,P0T).\mathbb{P}(D_{T}=1\mid F=1)\leq\mathbb{P}(D_{T}=1\mid F=0)+\TV(P_{1}^{T},P_{0}^{T}).

Here TV\TV denotes total variation distance.

Proposition 5 shows that feasible-side activity is impossible without observable separation. If a rule controls false release at level α\alpha, then Proposition 5 gives ℙ⁡(DT=1∣F=1)≤α+TV⁡(P1T,P0T)\mathbb{P}(D_{T}=1\mid F=1)\leq\alpha+\TV(P_{1}^{T},P_{0}^{T}). Thus any method that also achieves feasible-side release probability at least 1−β1-\beta must have TV⁡(P1T,P0T)≥1−β−α\TV(P_{1}^{T},P_{0}^{T})\geq 1-\beta-\alpha. This limitation is exactly why a power statement must impose some condition on the evidence supplied by feasible trajectories.

We therefore characterize feasible-side activity through the calibrated gain supplied by correct candidates. For this, fix a betting function in Algorithm 2 to a non-increasing f:[0,1]→(0,∞)f:[0,1]\to(0,\infty) satisfying ∫01f⁡(u)​𝑑u≤1\int_{0}^{1}f(u)\,du\leq 1. Define

Zt:=log⁡f⁡(pt)−log⁡f⁡(1)​ and ​Zmax:=log⁡f⁡(1n+1)−log⁡f⁡(1).\displaystyle Z_{t}:=\log f(p_{t})-\log f(1)\textrm{~and~}Z_{\max}:=\log f\!\left(\frac{1}{n+1}\right)-\log f(1).

The quantity ZtZ_{t} is the step-tt calibrated log-gain relative to the least favorable calibrated value p=1p=1. Since ff is non-increasing and pt∈[1/(n+1),1]p_{t}\in[1/(n+1),1], smaller ptp_{t}-values produce larger gains, and 0≤Zt≤Zmax.0\leq Z_{t}\leq Z_{\max}. Thus ZtZ_{t} measures how much evidence the current calibrated pp-value contributes beyond the baseline value f⁡(1)f(1), while ZmaxZ_{\max} is the largest possible one-step gain under the finite reference pool. Then the threshold Aα,T:=log⁡(1/α)−T​log⁡f⁡(1)A_{\alpha,T}:=\log(1/\alpha)-T\log f(1) is the cumulative calibrated gain needed for the terminal event ET≥1/αE_{T}\geq 1/\alpha. Indeed, under the fixed calibrator ff, ET=∏t=1Tf⁡(pt),E_{T}=\prod_{t=1}^{T}f(p_{t}), and hence log⁡ET=∑t=1Tlog⁡f⁡(pt)=∑t=1T{log⁡f⁡(1)+Zt}=T​log⁡f⁡(1)+∑t=1TZt.\log E_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log f(p_{t})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\{\log f(1)+Z_{t}\}=T\log f(1)+\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}. Therefore, ET≥1αE_{T}\geq\frac{1}{\alpha} if and only if ∑t=1TZt≥Aα,T.\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}\geq A_{\alpha,T}. In words, Aα,TA_{\alpha,T} is the amount of cumulative calibrated gain that must be accumulated by time TT for the terminal evidence to cross the release threshold.

Assumption 2 (Correct-candidate calibrated gain).

For a fixed horizon TT, assume that under F=1F=1, there exists a deterministic constant BT≥0B_{T}\geq 0 such that

∑t=1T𝔼[YtZt|𝒢~t−1,F=1]≥BTalmost surely.\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\!\left[Y_{t}Z_{t}\,\middle|\,\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=1\right]\geq B_{T}\qquad\text{almost surely}.

Assumption 2 says that, on feasible tasks, the workflow supplies enough correct-candidate calibrated gain over the first TT steps. The factor Yt∈{0,1}Y_{t}\in\{0,1\} ensures that only gain contributed by actually correct candidates is counted: when Yt=1Y_{t}=1, the candidate is correct and Yt​Zt=ZtY_{t}Z_{t}=Z_{t}; when Yt=0Y_{t}=0, the candidate is incorrect and Yt​Zt=0Y_{t}Z_{t}=0. Thus the assumption does not merely require favorable verifier scores in general. Rather, it requires that genuinely correct candidates contribute enough calibrated evidence, relative to the hard-negative reference pool, for the release threshold to be reachable within horizon TT.

This requirement is natural in applications such as coding agents. On a feasible coding task, once the workflow begins to generate correct or nearly correct programs, these candidates should tend to receive verifier scores that remain favorable relative to previously observed high-scoring failures. Even if no single step is decisive on its own, repeated appearances of such correct candidates can accumulate enough calibrated gain to support release. In this sense, Assumption 2 formalizes the idea that feasible trajectories should repeatedly produce not just high scores, but certifiably informative scores.

A useful interpretation is obtained by writing

πt:=ℙ⁡(Yt=1∣𝒢~t−1,F=1),Z¯t:=𝔼⁡(Zt∣𝒢~t−1,Yt=1,F=1),\pi_{t}:=\mathbb{P}(Y_{t}=1\mid\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=1),\qquad\bar{Z}_{t}:=\mathbb{E}(Z_{t}\mid\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},Y_{t}=1,F=1),

with the convention that πt​Z¯t=0\pi_{t}\bar{Z}_{t}=0 when πt=0\pi_{t}=0. Then

𝔼⁡(Yt​Zt∣𝒢~t−1,F=1)=πt​Z¯t.\mathbb{E}\!\left(Y_{t}Z_{t}\mid\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=1\right)=\pi_{t}\bar{Z}_{t}.

Here πt\pi_{t} is the conditional probability that the workflow reaches a correct candidate, while Z¯t\bar{Z}_{t} is the calibrated gain contributed by a correct candidate when one is reached. The first term reflects generation quality; the second reflects how strongly the evaluator and reference-pool calibration distinguish correct candidates from high-scoring failures. Accordingly, Assumption 2 requires the cumulative product of these two effects to be large enough.

Theorem 2 (Finite-horizon release power).

Assume Assumption 2. Let Δα,T=BT−Aα,T\Delta_{\alpha,T}=B_{T}-A_{\alpha,T}. If Δα,T>0\Delta_{\alpha,T}>0 and Zmax>0Z_{\max}>0, then

ℙ⁡(τα≤T∣F=1)≥1−exp⁡{−2​Δα,T2T​Zmax2}.\mathbb{P}(\tau_{\alpha}\leq T\mid F=1)\geq 1-\exp\!\left\{-\frac{2\Delta_{\alpha,T}^{2}}{TZ_{\max}^{2}}\right\}.

Theorem 2 compares the supplied correct-candidate gain BTB_{T} with the required gain Aα,TA_{\alpha,T}. If BTB_{T} exceeds Aα,TA_{\alpha,T}, then feasible trajectories provide enough expected calibrated evidence to clear the release threshold by time TT, up to a martingale concentration error. The margin Δα,T=BT−Aα,T\Delta_{\alpha,T}=B_{T}-A_{\alpha,T} controls the strength of this conclusion. Larger margins give a smaller exponential error term and hence a larger lower bound on ℙ⁡(τα≤T∣F=1)\mathbb{P}(\tau_{\alpha}\leq T\mid F=1). This is the sense in which the wrapper differs from an always-abstain rule. Under feasible trajectories that repeatedly supply positive calibrated gain from correct candidates, the same conservative rule can still cross the release threshold within the interaction horizon.

Remark 1 (Generator and verifier improvements).

Theorem 2 also describes how the wrapper should benefit as the underlying AI workflow improves. A stronger generator helps when it increases πt\pi_{t}, the chance that the workflow reaches a correct candidate. A stronger verifier helps when it increases Z¯t\bar{Z}_{t}, the calibrated gain assigned to correct candidates relative to the reference pool. Thus future improvements in AI translate into better release behavior only insofar as they increase the correct-candidate gain BTB_{T}. For fixed ff, nn, and TT, if an improved generator-verifier pair raises this lower bound from BTB_{T} to BT′≥BT+δB_{T}^{\prime}\geq B_{T}+\delta, then the release margin increases from Δα,T\Delta_{\alpha,T} to at least Δα,T+δ\Delta_{\alpha,T}+\delta. Overall, what matters is that correct candidates become more frequent, more separable from high-scoring failures, or both.

3.5 Calibration drift

The always-valid false-release control in Proposition 4 assumes exact failure-side calibration dominance. In deployment, however, repeated self-conditioning and other forms of history dependence may gradually shift the online score law away from the nominal calibration target. This subsection quantifies how such stepwise misspecification affects the false-release guarantee over a finite interaction horizon. Let P0P_{0} denote a nominal reference law for the stepwise pp-value stream, and under F=0F=0 let Qt,0=ℒ⁡(pt∣𝒢~t−1,F=0)Q_{t,0}=\mathcal{L}(p_{t}\mid\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=0).

Theorem 3 (Robustness to calibration drift).

Let et=f⁡(pt)∈[0,M]e_{t}=f(p_{t})\in[0,M], Et=∏j=1tejE_{t}=\prod_{j=1}^{t}e_{j}, and τα=inf{t≥1:Et≥1/α}\tau_{\alpha}=\inf\{t\geq 1:E_{t}\geq 1/\alpha\}, where ∫01f⁡(u)​P0​(𝑑u)≤1\int_{0}^{1}f(u)\,P_{0}(du)\leq 1. Assume that, under F=0F=0, TV⁡(Qt,0,P0)≤ϵ\TV(Q_{t,0},P_{0})\leq\epsilon almost surely for all t≥1t\geq 1. Then, for any T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N},

ℙ(τα≤T|σ(ℛ),F=0)≤α(1+Mϵ)T.\mathbb{P}\!\left(\tau_{\alpha}\leq T\,\middle|\,\sigma(\mathcal{R}),F=0\right)\leq\alpha(1+M\epsilon)^{T}.

Theorem 3 gives a finite-horizon view of calibration drift. In the normalized case M=1M=1, the inflation factor is (1+ϵ)T(1+\epsilon)^{T}, which is close to exp⁡(T​ϵ)\exp(T\epsilon) for small ϵ\epsilon. The relevant quantity is therefore the accumulated mismatch T​ϵT\epsilon, not the one-step mismatch alone. This is important in AI workflows because TT is the length of an interaction trajectory rather than an asymptotic sample size. In practice, this horizon is limited by token, latency, compute budgets, and engineering timeouts, which are already treated as operational constraints in coding-agent systems (Anthropic 2026b, Anthropic 2026c). The result therefore quantifies how finite-horizon safety degrades under small calibration drift, while making clear that such drift cannot be ignored over arbitrarily long interaction horizons.

4 Case Study: MBPP+ Code Generation

We study the proposed wrapper on MBPP+ (Mostly Basic Python Problems Plus), a code-generation benchmark (Austin et al. 2021, Liu et al. 2023). The benchmark provides a coding-agent instance of the broader workflow release problem: during deployment, the wrapper observes only a lightweight visible-test verifier, while offline correctness is assessed using a larger hidden test suite. This visible-hidden mismatch makes premature release a practical risk, since a generated program can receive a favorable visible score while still failing hidden tests. The case study therefore asks whether an adaptive generator-verifier workflow can accumulate enough calibrated evidence to release without relying on raw verifier scores alone.

Our implementation uses Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (Hui et al. 2024) with max_new_tokens=240, temperature=0.7, and top_p=0.95. For each task, the model generates a trajectory of ten sequential candidates, with one candidate produced at each step. Throughout the main analysis, the online verifier score St∈[0,1]S_{t}\in[0,1] is the empirical pass rate on a visible subset of unit tests. The wrapper observes only this visible score stream and must decide whether to release or abstain. Sections A and B of the Supplementary Material provide implementation details and additional numerical results.

4.1 Task curation, visible-hidden split, and empirical regimes

Each MBPP+ task is a Python coding problem consisting of four components:

  1. 1.

    Prompt: A natural-language instruction describing the desired logic.

  2. 2.

    Entry point: The exact function name the LLM is required to implement.

  3. 3.

    Canonical solution: A human-verified reference implementation.

  4. 4.

    Test cases: A collection of input-output pairs used to evaluate generated code.

In our study, the test cases are partitioned into two disjoint subsets. The first serves as a visible verifier, providing a lightweight online signal to score candidates during deployment. The second acts as a stronger hidden oracle for offline evaluation. This visible-hidden split creates the central practical challenge: a generated program may achieve a highly favorable visible score yet fail the hidden tests, rendering the online verifier informative but imperfect.

The following representative task illustrates this mismatch. It also helps explain why selective release is nontrivial in code generation.

Representative MBPP+ task: structural pattern matching. Task Mbpp/74 asks whether two sequences follow the same structural pattern. This type of task is vulnerable to verifier mismatch because a limited visible test subset may capture only basic positive or negative matches while missing important edge cases such as length mismatches, repeated sub-patterns, or empty-list behavior. As a result, a structurally flawed candidate can overfit the visible verifier and obtain a deceptively high score while still failing the hidden oracle.

To standardize evaluation, we retain only tasks with at least 100100 usable tests, where a usable test is one passed by the canonical solution. For each retained task, we deterministically select 100100 tests. These are partitioned into 3030 visible verifier tests and 7070 hidden evaluation tests. The visible tests are used to compute the online verifier score, while the hidden tests are used only for offline evaluation and empirical feasibility labeling. The main paper focuses on the Ntest=30N_{\mathrm{test}}=30 setting; reduced verifier sizes Ntest∈{10,20}N_{\mathrm{test}}\in\{10,20\} are discussed in Supplementary Section B.2 for robustness analysis.

We further partition the curated tasks into three disjoint subsets. The bank split is used only for constructing candidate reference pools and calibrating the entropy baseline. The select split is used only for diagnosing candidate reference-pool families. The final split is reserved exclusively for held-out reporting. This separation is important: the final evaluation is not used to choose the pool family, and the select split is not used for final performance reporting. In the present study, the selected family is top55, which retains the upper 55%55\% of executable incorrect bank-step scores, with ties included at the quantile cutoff.

Because true algorithmic correctness is not available in an absolute sense, we define empirical correctness by whether a generated candidate passes all 7070 hidden tests. Based on this hidden-test evaluation over the full ten-step trajectory, we partition the held-out tasks into an empirical infeasible subset F0F_{0} and an empirical feasible subset F1F_{1}. The subset F0F_{0} contains tasks for which no correct candidate ever appears, while F1F_{1} contains tasks for which at least one correct candidate appears. On F0F_{0}, every release is necessarily an error, so the release rate coincides with the false-release rate. On F1F_{1}, the release rate serves as a power-style companion metric, while the release-conditional failure rate measures the reliability of released outputs.

4.2 Baselines

We compare the proposed wrapper with three baselines motivated by existing stopping heuristics. More details of these baselines are deferred to the Supplementary Section A.

  • •

    First_p. A single-step calibrated stopping rule, defined by

    τ=inf{t:pt≤α}.\tau=\inf\{t:p_{t}\leq\alpha\}.

    This baseline uses the same calibrated pp-values and the same reference pool as our method, but without sequential evidence accumulation.

  • •

    Entropy. A predictive-confidence baseline based on entropy (Sharma and Chopra 2025): It releases once the candidate’s mean entropy falls below a threshold estimated from correctly generated bank-split candidates.

  • •

    Stability. A short-run score-convergence baseline motivated by recent stopping heuristics based on response stability (Li et al. 2024, Mao et al. 2025). It releases when the visible verifier score becomes sufficiently stable at a sufficiently high level.

The Entropy and Stability baselines do not depend on α\alpha or on the reference pool. The First_p baseline isolates the role of sequential accumulation by using the same calibrated pp-values as our method but making a release decision from a single step rather than from accumulated evidence. In our experiments, the method in Xie et al. (2026) is not applicable because their method relies on token-level uncertainty signals from reasoning traces and targets early stopping for well-posed queries, whereas our framework is designed as a black-box wrapper for false-release control.

A useful point of reference is the degenerate rule that always abstains. Such a rule trivially guarantees zero false releases, but it also yields a feasible-side release rate of zero and is therefore uninformative in practice. Accordingly, our evaluation tracks not only false-release control on F0F_{0}, but also feasible-side activity on F1F_{1}, so that conservative behavior is not confused with useful deployment performance.

4.3 Reference-pool construction and held-out selection

Following Section 3.2, we construct candidate reference pools from incorrect trajectories in the bank split, retaining only the upper tail of the visible verifier score. A broad pool such as all_incorrect, which includes every incorrect candidate regardless of its score, dilutes the failure-side upper tail with easy negatives and makes online scores appear artificially extreme. At the opposite extreme, overly restrictive pools such as top35 or top45 may become too conservative and suppress feasible-side release within the ten-step horizon. We therefore use the select split to choose a practical compromise.

Figure 3 reports the select-stage diagnostic at Ntest=30N_{\mathrm{test}}=30. The broad pool all_incorrect is visibly anti-conservative. As the retained pool is restricted to harder negatives, the induced empirical upper-tail pp-values move below the diagonal, indicating increasingly conservative calibration. Among the candidate families considered in the main paper, top55 is the most relaxed pool that passes the held-out diagnostic. Stricter pools do not yield an obvious additional safety benefit in this diagnostic, while relaxing the threshold further produces visible lower-tail inflation. We therefore use top55 in all subsequent main-paper evaluations. Supplement Section B.1 reports a broader sensitivity analysis over candidate upper-tail families. It confirms that top55 is the least conservative choice among those considered that still passes the held-out diagnostic.

4.4 Evaluation of false-release control and feasible-side release

Table 1 reports the held-out results at Ntest=30N_{\mathrm{test}}=30 using the selected top55 reference pool. On the empirical infeasible subset F0F_{0}, the primary metric is the false-release rate. On the empirical feasible subset F1F_{1}, we report the release rate, the release-conditional failure rate, and the average release step.

The heuristic baselines Entropy and Stability exhibit elevated false-release rates under F0F_{0}. The entropy rule relies on point-in-time predictive confidence, while the stability rule relies on short-run smoothness of the visible pass rate. In this setting, neither local confidence nor local smoothness is sufficient to protect against spuriously favorable verifier signals from structurally incorrect candidates. Their false-release rates on F0F_{0} are 0.76670.7667 and 0.23330.2333, respectively. The First_p baseline isolates the role of the decision layer, since it applies a one-step threshold to the exact same calibrated pp-values used by our e-process. Under the selected hard-negative pool, the induced pp-value scale is discrete. In the main setting, because the selected pool of 170 hard negatives already contains 24 incorrect bank steps with perfect visible scores, even a flawless 30/30 maps only to pt=(1+24)/(170+1)≈0.146p_{t}=(1+24)/(170+1)\approx 0.146. Consequently, at the more relaxed threshold α=0.20\alpha=0.20, First_p is highly active: it releases on 99.32% of feasible tasks, but this aggressiveness comes with a false-release rate of 0.0667 on F0F_{0}. At stricter levels, however, it encounters a sharp utility cliff. When α∈{0.10,0.05}\alpha\in\{0.10,0.05\}, no single calibrated step is sufficient for release, and the method becomes inactive on feasible held-out tasks. In this benchmark, the limitation of a one-step calibrated rule is therefore not only its vulnerability to spurious early signals under F0F_{0}, but also the resolution limit it faces under F1F_{1}.

By contrast, the proposed wrapper overcomes this limit by accumulating repeated moderate evidence across the trajectory. At α=0.10\alpha=0.10, it yields zero false releases on F0F_{0} and zero release-conditional failures on F1F_{1}, while maintaining a feasible-side release rate of 0.7703. At α=0.05\alpha=0.05, it remains active on 74.32% of feasible tasks, with a release-conditional failure rate of 0.0091. This improvement comes at the cost of later release: because the e-process requires sustained favorable evidence to cross the threshold, the average release step is naturally delayed relative to more aggressive one-step rules. Overall, the comparison shows that sequential accumulation preserves useful feasible-side activity precisely where one-step calibrated stopping breaks down.

This comparison also illustrates the role of Theorem 2. False-release control alone would be achieved by an always-abstain rule, but such a rule has no feasible-side activity. The proposed wrapper is different: at α=0.10\alpha=0.10, it has zero false release on F0F_{0} while still releasing on 77.03%77.03\% of F1F_{1} tasks. The empirical mechanism is consistent with the gain-based interpretation in Theorem 2. Release does not require a single decisive calibrated step; repeated favorable candidates can supply enough cumulative calibrated gain to cross the evidence threshold.

4.5 Representative task trajectories

Aggregate metrics alone do not fully reveal how the wrapper behaves along individual reasoning trajectories. We therefore examine two representative held-out tasks at α=0.10\alpha=0.10, chosen to illustrate the two main operating modes of the method: safe abstention under persistent verifier deception and delayed correct release through evidence accumulation.

Safe abstention under persistent verifier deception. Task Mbpp/74 asks whether two sequences follow the same pattern structure. In this type of structural matching problem, a limited visible test subset may miss failures involving length, alignment, or repeated-subpattern logic. In the observed trajectory, no correct candidate ever appears under the hidden oracle, yet the visible verifier score remains 0.9670.967 throughout. Both Entropy and Stability are triggered by these persistently favorable local signals and release incorrectly. Under the selected hard-negative pool, however, the score calibrates to pt=0.216p_{t}=0.216, which is not especially extreme relative to previously observed deceptive failures. As a result, the accumulated evidence grows only gradually, reaching 5.4695.469 by the terminal step and never crossing the release threshold of 1010. In this case, the wrapper avoids false release because it evaluates the score relative to a benchmark of strong failures rather than relying on its raw magnitude alone.

Correct release through repeated moderate evidence. The task Mbpp/598 asks whether an integer is an Armstrong number. Such arithmetic predicate tasks are prone to partial overfitting: a flawed rule may perform well on the visible verifier subset while failing under the hidden oracle. At t=1t=1, an incorrect candidate receives a visible score of 0.8670.867, which prompts Entropy to release incorrectly. From t=2t=2 onward, the generated logic is correct and the visible score is 1.0001.000. Under the selected hard-negative pool, however, even a perfect visible score maps only to pt=0.146p_{t}=0.146. While this is sufficient for Stability to release at t=3t=3, it remains strictly above the α=0.10\alpha=0.10 threshold for First_p, which therefore never releases despite the task being effectively solved from t=2t=2 onward. The proposed wrapper succeeds by accumulating this repeated moderate evidence over time. As the correct candidate continues to appear, the wealth process grows from 1.4761.476 to 13.61713.617, crossing the release threshold at t=7t=7. In the notation of Theorem 2, this is a trajectory where no single calibrated step is decisive, but the repeated correct candidates after t=2t=2 contribute positive calibrated gains ZtZ_{t}. The release at t=7t=7 is therefore a cumulative-gain crossing rather than a one-step threshold crossing.

Overall, the MBPP+ case study illustrates the two main operating characteristics of the wrapper. On empirically infeasible trajectories, it resists repeated but non-decisive verifier spikes and avoids premature release. On empirically feasible trajectories, it remains active by accumulating moderate evidence across steps until the evidence threshold is crossed. The examples show how the wrapper can abstain under persistent verifier deception while still releasing when useful calibrated evidence appears repeatedly over the trajectory.

5 Conclusion

We studied release decisions for black-box generate-verify AI workflows, where the central question is when evidence accumulated along an adaptive trajectory is strong enough to justify releasing an output. We formulated this as a sequential selective-release problem. The proposed wrapper separates score calibration from evidence accumulation. A hard-negative reference pool converts adaptive verifier scores into calibrated evidence, and an e-process accumulates that evidence under optional stopping. This yields finite-sample false-release control under a failure-side dominance condition and explains how the same conservative rule can remain active on feasible instances through repeated calibrated gain. In the MBPP+ case study, the wrapper reduced premature incorrect release relative to heuristic stopping rules while preserving feasible-side release through evidence accumulation.

More broadly, AI-assisted decision-making is creating new statistical objects beyond fixed datasets and one-shot predictions. This paper studies one such setting, but many others are likely to arise. A central opportunity for statistics would be to develop principled decision rules for these new structures, especially when classical assumptions are unavailable.

“When Should an AI Workflow Release?
Always-Valid Inference for Black-Box Generate-Verify Systems”

This supplementary material provides the implementation details, auxiliary diagnostics, and proofs that support the main text.

    Section A documents the MBPP+ case-study implementation, including representative tasks, task curation, visible-hidden test construction, empirical feasible and infeasible subsets, baseline rules, and computational environment.
