    Section C delivers the proofs of the formal results in the main paper.

Appendix A Details on the MBPP+ Case Study

This section records the benchmark-specific implementation details behind the MBPP+ case study. It begins with two additional representative task specifications that complement the main-text example, then describes how usable input-output pairs are curated and split into visible-verifier and hidden-oracle sets. The subsequent subsections explain the bank, select, and final task splits, the empirical construction of feasible and infeasible held-out subsets, the entropy and stability baselines, and the computational environment used to generate and evaluate the cached trajectories.

A.1 Additional representative MBPP+ tasks

The main text introduces the MBPP+ setup and Mbpp/74 as a representative example. Here we record the remaining task specifications used in the analysis, Mbpp/598 and Mbpp/643.

Task Mbpp/598: Out-of-Distribution Arithmetic. Detecting an Armstrong number is an arithmetic predicate problem. Simple heuristic logic often passes the small integers present in the verifier subset. However, structural flaws in the model’s arithmetic reasoning are aggressively exposed by the unusually large integers (e.g., 20-digit numbers).

Task Mbpp/643: Boundary Logic and Regex. This task involves checking if ‘z’ appears inside a word, not at the boundaries. A candidate code might capture local patterns correctly on the verifier but fail on the edge-case.

A.2 Task curation and pair construction

From the MBPP+ benchmark, we retain only tasks with at least 100100 usable input-output pairs. For each retained task, we deterministically select 100100 pairs. This curation step standardizes the task-level evaluation budget across tasks and removes variability caused purely by heterogeneous raw pair counts. It also fixes the downstream task partition and prevents numerical comparisons from being driven by shifting task-specific evaluation sizes.

For each curated task, we reserve 7070 oracle-label pairs and 3030 verifier pairs. The oracle-label set is used only for empirical feasibility labeling and final correctness evaluation. The verifier score is computed from a prefix of the 3030 verifier pairs, which yields the aligned settings Ntest∈{10,20,30}N_{\mathrm{test}}\in\{10,20,30\}. Throughout, the main setting is Ntest=30N_{\mathrm{test}}=30.

A.3 Task splits and their roles

We partition the curated tasks into a bank split, a select split, and a final split. The bank split is used only for reference-pool construction and for entropy-threshold calibration. The select split is used only for diagnosis of candidate pool families. The final split is used only for held-out reporting. This separation is important. The diagnosis stage is not a reporting stage, and the final evaluation is not used to choose the pool family.

In the present study, the final selected family is top55, which retains the upper 55%55\% of executable incorrect bank steps, with ties included at the quantile cutoff. The broad family all_incorrect is used only as a diagnostic baseline.

A.4 Empirical F0F_{0} and F1F_{1}

For a fixed task trajectory, the empirical infeasibility subset F0F_{0} consists of tasks for which no correct candidate ever appears under the oracle-label set. The empirical feasible subset F1F_{1} consists of tasks for which at least one correct candidate appears. On F0F_{0}, every release is necessarily wrong, so the release rate coincides with the false-release rate. On F1F_{1}, the release rate serves as a power-style companion metric, while the release-conditional failure rate measures the reliability of released outputs.

A.5 Detail on Baseline Methods

We compare the proposed wrapper with two heuristic stopping rules.

Predictive entropy. For candidate CtC_{t}, let HtH_{t} denote the mean token-level entropy,

Ht=1Lt∑j=1Lt(−∑v∈𝒱Kπ^t,j(v)logπ^t,j(v)),H_{t}=\frac{1}{L_{t}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{t}}\left(-\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{K}}\hat{\pi}_{t,j}(v)\log\hat{\pi}_{t,j}(v)\right),

where π^t,j\hat{\pi}_{t,j} is the predictive distribution over the top-KK tokens at position jj, with K=50K=50 in our experiments, and LtL_{t} is the sequence length. Let hh be the mean entropy over correctly generated candidates in the bank split. The entropy baseline releases at

τent:=inf{t≥1:Ht≤h},\tau_{\mathrm{ent}}:=\inf\{t\geq 1:H_{t}\leq h\},

with abstention if this event does not occur within the maximum horizon.

Algorithmic stability. This rule releases once the observed verifier score becomes sufficiently stable at a high level. Define

Δt:=maxj∈{t−1,t}⁡Sj−minj∈{t−1,t}⁡Sj.\Delta_{t}:=\max_{j\in\{t-1,t\}}S_{j}-\min_{j\in\{t-1,t\}}S_{j}.

For a verifier using NtestN_{\mathrm{test}} visible tests, the stability baseline releases at

τstab:=inf{t≥2:Δt≤1/Ntest​ and ​St≥0.8},\tau_{\mathrm{stab}}:=\inf\{t\geq 2:\Delta_{t}\leq 1/N_{\mathrm{test}}\text{ and }S_{t}\geq 0.8\},

with abstention otherwise. The tolerance 1/Ntest1/N_{\mathrm{test}} corresponds to one visible test on the discrete verifier-score scale.

Computational environment. All computational experiments were implemented in Python, and the code-generation task was run on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. The main computational cost lies in generating and caching the task trajectories. Once the trajectories and verifier scores are recorded, the wrapper evaluation, baseline comparisons, and certifiable-gain diagnostics are performed offline and add negligible additional cost.

Appendix B Additional Results on MBPP+ Benchmark

This section complements the main MBPP+ analysis in four directions. Section B.1 broadens the select-stage diagnosis over a wider range of upper-tail pool families. Section B.2 reports robustness checks for verifier resolution and betting aggressiveness. Section B.3 gives an additional task-level trajectory illustrating oscillating feasible-side success. Section B.4 outlines cached-trajectory certifiable-gain diagnostics that connect the feasible-side power analysis to the same MBPP+ trajectories used in the case study.

B.1 Broader diagnosis over candidate reference-pool families

The main text reports the select-stage diagnosis for a small set of candidate families centered around top55. Table S1 broadens this search to all_incorrect, top35, top45, top55, top65, top75, and top85, and reports the empirical lower-tail probabilities of the induced upper-tail pp-values on the select-stage empirical F0F_{0} subset.

The broad pool all_incorrect is anti-conservative throughout. At the main setting Ntest=30N_{\mathrm{test}}=30, it yields Pr^​(p≤0.10)=0.1136\widehat{\Pr}(p\leq 0.10)=0.1136 and Pr^​(p≤0.20)=0.4205\widehat{\Pr}(p\leq 0.20)=0.4205, well above the corresponding values for the harder upper-tail families. As the retained bank is restricted to stronger negatives, the induced upper tail becomes more conservative. This shift is useful only up to a point. More aggressive families suppress false release more strongly, but they also raise the baseline pp-values and make feasible-side release harder. In the main Ntest=30N_{\mathrm{test}}=30 regime, the families from top35 through top55 all yield Pr^​(p≤0.20)=0.1136\widehat{\Pr}(p\leq 0.20)=0.1136, while top65 already increases this value to 0.21590.2159. This is the numerical pattern behind the main-text choice of top55. It is the most relaxed family in this reduced grid that remains within the acceptable range under the held-out select-stage diagnosis.

B.2 Robustness to practical design choices

We examine the robustness of the proposed wrapper to two practical design choices: the resolution of the visible verifier, NtestN_{\mathrm{test}}, and the betting exponent, η\eta. Table S2 demonstrates that greater conservativeness in either dimension improves protection against false release, but it also delays or reduces feasible-side activity.

We first vary the verifier resolution with Ntest∈{10,20,30}N_{\mathrm{test}}\in\{10,20,30\}, while keeping the selected reference-pool family fixed at top55. As Panel A shows, reducing NtestN_{\mathrm{test}} coarsens the discrete pp-value scale and correspondingly weakens the strength of the calibrated evidence. At Ntest=20N_{\mathrm{test}}=20, the wrapper remains active at α=0.20\alpha=0.20 and 0.100.10, although feasible-side releases occur noticeably later than in the main Ntest=30N_{\mathrm{test}}=30 setting. At Ntest=10N_{\mathrm{test}}=10, the degradation is more pronounced: the resolution becomes so coarse that the accumulated wealth no longer reaches the stricter release thresholds (α∈{0.10,0.05}\alpha\in\{0.10,0.05\}) within the ten-step horizon, rendering the method inactive on feasible tasks. The infeasible-side results move much less dramatically, indicating that a coarser verifier primarily reduces feasible-side utility rather than materially weakening false-release control.

We next vary the betting exponent η∈{0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9}\eta\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9\} under the selected top55 family at the main verifier setting Ntest=30N_{\mathrm{test}}=30. Panel B shows a complementary trade-off. Smaller values produce a more conservative wealth process and can make the method inactive at stringent thresholds. Larger values lead to earlier and more frequent releases, but they also weaken the empirical safety margin on infeasible tasks. In particular, the aggressive choice η=0.9\eta=0.9 accelerates release but incurs nonzero false release on F0F_{0} already at α=0.10\alpha=0.10, whereas η=0.3\eta=0.3 is so conservative that it becomes inactive at α∈{0.10,0.05}\alpha\in\{0.10,0.05\}. Among the values considered, η=0.7\eta=0.7 provides the most stable compromise, maintaining substantial feasible-side activity while preserving strong infeasible-side control in the main setting.

These robustness patterns are also consistent with Theorem 2. Reducing NtestN_{\mathrm{test}} coarsens the verifier score and weakens the calibrated separation between correct candidates and hard negatives, making it harder for the cumulative gain to exceed Aα,TA_{\alpha,T} within ten steps. Increasing η\eta enlarges the gain scale ZtZ_{t}, which can improve feasible-side activity, but the same aggressiveness can reduce the empirical safety margin on F0F_{0}.

These robustness results support the design choices used in the main analysis. A moderately resolved verifier is important for maintaining informative evidence accumulation, and η=0.7\eta=0.7 provides a stable empirical compromise between infeasible-side safety and feasible-side release.

B.3 Additional task-level trajectory

To complement the main trace analysis, Table S3 records one additional feasible-side trajectory whose verifier signal is high but not a monotone certificate of correctness. The example is useful precisely because it exposes the cost and the benefit of the conservative anytime-valid wrapper: it may not release at the first correct candidate, but when it does release, the selected candidate is correct.

Table S3 studies Mbpp/643, which asks whether a string contains the letter ‘z’ away from both word boundaries. Boundary-sensitive text-matching tasks admit many partially correct rules. A candidate may capture the broad pattern of interior occurrences while still mishandling edge cases involving initial or terminal positions, repeated z’s, or boundary-adjacent matches. This makes high visible scores possible even when the candidate logic is still incorrect.

This trajectory also illustrates the cost of our conservative decision rule. The first candidate is already oracle-correct, and Entropy releases correctly at this point. Our wrapper does not release immediately, because even a perfect visible score corresponds to a calibrated value pt=0.146p_{t}=0.146 under the selected top55 null pool, which is above the nominal α=0.10\alpha=0.10 one-step release threshold. This is an intentional consequence of calibrating against strong hard-negative candidates rather than treating a raw score of 1.0001.000 as automatically decisive.

The same trajectory shows why this conservatism can be useful. Immediately after the first correct candidate, the next three candidates have high visible scores 0.9670.967 but are incorrect under the hidden oracle. The Stability rule releases at t=2t=2 after a short high-score window, and that release is an error. Later, correctness continues to alternate: steps 55 and 77 are correct, step 88 is incorrect, and steps 99 and 1010 are correct. Thus, local score smoothness and high raw verifier scores are informative but not decisive in this example.

The proposed wrapper responds differently. It does not claim the earliest correct candidate, but it continues to accumulate calibrated evidence across the trajectory. Since every single-step value remains above α=0.10\alpha=0.10, First_p never releases. In contrast, the wealth process eventually crosses the anytime threshold 1/α=101/\alpha=10, reaching Et=13.831E_{t}=13.831 at t=9t=9. The candidate selected at this first crossing time is oracle-correct. This example therefore highlights a central tradeoff of the method: conservative calibration can delay release even when an early candidate is correct, but the actual release event is tied to accumulated evidence and occurs here on a true candidate rather than on the intervening high-score failures.

B.4 Certifiable-gain diagnostics for feasible-side release

Theorem 2 identifies calibrated gain from correct candidates as the central feasible-side quantity. The cached MBPP+ trajectories allow this quantity to be measured post hoc, because each candidate has both a calibrated verifier-derived pp-value and a hidden-oracle correctness label. We therefore compute trajectory-level gain decompositions that separate the evidence observed by the wrapper from the portion attributable to oracle-correct candidates.

B.4.1 Trajectory-level gain decomposition

For a fixed betting function ff, define the calibrated gain Zt=log⁡f⁡(pt)−log⁡f⁡(1)Z_{t}=\log f(p_{t})-\log f(1), the cumulative observed gain Gt=∑j=1tZjG_{t}=\sum_{j=1}^{t}Z_{j}, the cumulative correct-candidate gain Gt+=∑j=1tYj​ZjG_{t}^{+}=\sum_{j=1}^{t}Y_{j}Z_{j}, and the required cumulative gain Aα,t=log⁡(1/α)−t​log⁡f⁡(1)A_{\alpha,t}=\log(1/\alpha)-t\log f(1). The release condition satisfies

Et≥1/α⟺Gt≥Aα,t.E_{t}\geq 1/\alpha\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G_{t}\geq A_{\alpha,t}.

The wrapper observes GtG_{t}, since it is determined by the online calibrated pp-values. The quantity Gt+G_{t}^{+} is a post hoc attribution using hidden-oracle labels, measuring the portion of observed gain contributed by oracle-correct candidates. It is not used by the wrapper during deployment.

We also record the maximum observed margin and maximum correct-candidate margin,

M⁡(x):=maxt≤Tmax⁡{Gt​(x)−Aα,t},M+​(x):=maxt≤Tmax⁡{Gt+​(x)−Aα,t}.M(x):=\max_{t\leq T_{\max}}\{G_{t}(x)-A_{\alpha,t}\},\qquad M^{+}(x):=\max_{t\leq T_{\max}}\{G_{t}^{+}(x)-A_{\alpha,t}\}.

These margins summarize whether a trajectory ever supplies enough observed gain, or enough correct-candidate gain, to exceed the required gain curve. In the notation of Theorem 2, BTB_{T} is a conditional expected gain lower bound rather than an observed trajectory-level quantity. The diagnostics Gt+G_{t}^{+} and M+M^{+} provide empirical, post hoc analogues for examining the mechanism behind feasible-side release. All quantities in this subsection are computed from the cached trajectories without regenerating model outputs or rerunning tests.

Figure S1 and Table S4 show three distinct gain patterns. For Mbpp/74, no candidate is correct under the hidden oracle, so Gt+=0G_{t}^{+}=0 throughout. The raw verifier scores are persistently high enough to generate some observed gain, but GT=10.72G_{T}=10.72 remains below the required terminal gain Aα,T=11.32A_{\alpha,T}=11.32, and the maximum observed margin is negative. This is the gain-level representation of safe abstention.

For Mbpp/598, the hidden oracle labels the candidates correct from the second step onward. The correct-candidate gain therefore rises nearly in parallel with the observed gain, with GT+=12.11G_{T}^{+}=12.11 accounting for 93.5%93.5\% of terminal observed gain. The observed path crosses the threshold at t=7t=7, and the selected candidate is correct. This is the cleanest instance of the mechanism in Theorem 2: individually moderate calibrated evidence becomes decisive after repeated correct candidates.

The Mbpp/643 trajectory is more nuanced and complements the trace in Table S3. The wrapper releases correctly at t=9t=9, but GT+=6.73G_{T}^{+}=6.73 is well below Aα,T=11.32A_{\alpha,T}=11.32, and M+<0M^{+}<0. Thus the crossing is not explained by correct-candidate gain alone; high-scoring incorrect candidates also contribute observed calibrated evidence. This distinction is substantively informative: GtG_{t} is the online evidence process used by the wrapper, while Gt+G_{t}^{+} is the hidden-oracle attribution of that evidence. The release event is still tied to a valid threshold crossing, and in this trajectory the first crossing occurs at a true candidate, but the path exposes the cost and structure of conservative calibrated stopping in an oscillating feasible task.

B.4.2 Held-out feasible-side gain diagnostics

The held-out feasible-side summaries in Figure S2 and Table S5 show that release activity is strongly aligned with the accumulation of correct-candidate gain.

Among the 148 feasible tasks in the main setting, the wrapper releases on 114. These released tasks have mean observed margin 1.931.93 and mean correct-gain margin 1.801.80, whereas the 34 abstained feasible tasks have mean margins −2.01-2.01 and −2.30-2.30, respectively. Moreover, 95.6%95.6\% of released feasible tasks have M+>0M^{+}>0, compared with 0%0\% of abstained feasible tasks. The small difference between MM and M+M^{+} for the released group also indicates that, in aggregate, the observed threshold crossings are mostly supplied by candidates that are correct under the hidden oracle.

Table S6 makes the decomposition in Theorem 2 concrete. The empirical correct-candidate frequency is high throughout the ten-step horizon, ranging from 0.810.81 to 0.860.86. Conditional on correctness, the mean calibrated gain is stable at about 1.341.34, reflecting the fact that correct candidates are typically assigned near-perfect verifier scores under the top55 calibration. The resulting cumulative mean correct gain reaches 11.2311.23 by T=10T=10, nearly matching the required terminal gain Aα,T=11.32A_{\alpha,T}=11.32. This near equality explains why the main setting is active but not overly aggressive: feasible tasks often supply enough calibrated gain to cross the threshold, but there remains a nontrivial abstention region when the correct-candidate gain arrives too late or too weakly.

B.4.3 Gain sensitivity to verifier resolution and betting strength

The sensitivity results in Figure S3 and Table S7 align with the two sources of feasible-side power highlighted by Theorem 2.

Increasing NtestN_{\mathrm{test}} sharpens the calibrated separation between correct candidates and the hard-negative pool. At α=0.10\alpha=0.10 and η=0.7\eta=0.7, the mean terminal correct gain increases from 9.009.00 at Ntest=10N_{\mathrm{test}}=10 to 11.2311.23 at Ntest=30N_{\mathrm{test}}=30, and the mean correct-gain margin moves from −1.23-1.23 to 0.860.86. The feasible-side release rate correspondingly rises from 00 to 0.770.77. Varying η\eta changes the gain scale directly. At Ntest=30N_{\mathrm{test}}=30, increasing η\eta from 0.30.3 to 0.90.9 raises mean GT+G_{T}^{+} from 4.814.81 to 14.4414.44 and accelerates release. This power gain is not free: as shown in the main robustness table, the most aggressive setting η=0.9\eta=0.9 also introduces nonzero false release on F0F_{0} at α=0.10\alpha=0.10. The selected η=0.7\eta=0.7 therefore sits in the empirical region where correct-candidate gain is large enough for substantial feasible-side activity while preserving the stronger infeasible-side safety margin observed in the main setting.

Appendix C Proofs

This section presents detailed proofs for the theoretical results established in the main text, organized in the order of their appearance.

C.1 Proof of Proposition 1

If ℙ⁡(D=1)=0\mathbb{P}(D=1)=0, the release-conditional quantity is vacuous. We therefore consider the nondegenerate case ℙ⁡(D=1)>0\mathbb{P}(D=1)>0. Write

q:=ℙ⁡(Yτ=0∣D=1,F=1),β:=ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=1).q:=\mathbb{P}(Y_{\tau}=0\mid D=1,F=1),\qquad\beta:=\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=1).

If ℙ⁡(D=1,F=1)=0\mathbb{P}(D=1,F=1)=0, qq may be defined arbitrarily in [0,1][0,1], since it is multiplied below by ℙ⁡(F=1∣D=1)=0\mathbb{P}(F=1\mid D=1)=0.

Step 1. Decompose the release-conditional failure rate by feasibility. By the law of total probability conditional on {D=1}\{D=1\},

ℙ⁡(Yτ=0∣D=1)=ℙ⁡(Yτ=0∣D=1,F=0)​ℙ​(F=0∣D=1)+q​ℙ​(F=1∣D=1).\mathbb{P}(Y_{\tau}=0\mid D=1)=\mathbb{P}(Y_{\tau}=0\mid D=1,F=0)\mathbb{P}(F=0\mid D=1)+q\,\mathbb{P}(F=1\mid D=1).

Also,

{ℙ⁡(Yτ=0∣D=1,F=0)≤1,ℙ⁡(F=1∣D=1)=1−ℙ⁡(F=0∣D=1).\left\{\begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(Y_{\tau}=0\mid D=1,F=0)&\leq 1,\\ \mathbb{P}(F=1\mid D=1)&=1-\mathbb{P}(F=0\mid D=1).\end{aligned}\right.

Substituting these two facts into the preceding display gives

ℙ⁡(Yτ=0∣D=1)≤ℙ⁡(F=0∣D=1)+q⁡{1−ℙ⁡(F=0∣D=1)}.\mathbb{P}(Y_{\tau}=0\mid D=1)\leq\mathbb{P}(F=0\mid D=1)+q\{1-\mathbb{P}(F=0\mid D=1)\}.

Rearranging the right-hand side,

ℙ⁡(F=0∣D=1)+q⁡{1−ℙ⁡(F=0∣D=1)}=q+(1−q)​ℙ​(F=0∣D=1).\mathbb{P}(F=0\mid D=1)+q\{1-\mathbb{P}(F=0\mid D=1)\}=q+(1-q)\mathbb{P}(F=0\mid D=1).

Thus

Rout=ℙ⁡(Yτ=0∣D=1)≤q+(1−q)​ℙ​(F=0∣D=1).R_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb{P}(Y_{\tau}=0\mid D=1)\leq q+(1-q)\mathbb{P}(F=0\mid D=1).

Step 2. Bound the posterior probability of infeasibility after release. By Bayes’ rule,

ℙ⁡(F=0∣D=1)=ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=0)​ℙ​(F=0)ℙ⁡(D=1).\mathbb{P}(F=0\mid D=1)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=0)\mathbb{P}(F=0)}{\mathbb{P}(D=1)}.

Using π0=ℙ⁡(F=0)\pi_{0}=\mathbb{P}(F=0) and decomposing ℙ⁡(D=1)\mathbb{P}(D=1) over F∈{0,1}F\in\{0,1\},

ℙ⁡(D=1)=ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=0)​ℙ​(F=0)+ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=1)​ℙ​(F=1).\mathbb{P}(D=1)=\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=0)\mathbb{P}(F=0)+\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=1)\mathbb{P}(F=1).

Since ℙ⁡(F=1)=1−π0\mathbb{P}(F=1)=1-\pi_{0} and β=ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=1)\beta=\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=1), this becomes

ℙ⁡(D=1)=π0​ℙ​(D=1∣F=0)+(1−π0)​β.\mathbb{P}(D=1)=\pi_{0}\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=0)+(1-\pi_{0})\beta.

Substituting this denominator into Bayes’ rule gives

ℙ⁡(F=0∣D=1)=π0​ℙ​(D=1∣F=0)π0​ℙ​(D=1∣F=0)+(1−π0)​β.\mathbb{P}(F=0\mid D=1)=\frac{\pi_{0}\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=0)}{\pi_{0}\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=0)+(1-\pi_{0})\beta}.

Step 3. Substitute the infeasibility bound into the risk decomposition. From Step 1,

Rout≤q+(1−q)​ℙ​(F=0∣D=1).R_{\mathrm{out}}\leq q+(1-q)\mathbb{P}(F=0\mid D=1).

Using the bound from Step 2,

{q=ℙ⁡(Yτ=0∣D=1,F=1),β=ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=1),\left\{\begin{aligned} q&=\mathbb{P}(Y_{\tau}=0\mid D=1,F=1),\\ \beta&=\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=1),\end{aligned}\right.

we obtain

Rout≤ℙ⁡(Yτ=0∣D=1,F=1)+(1−ℙ⁡(Yτ=0∣D=1,F=1))​π0​απ0​α+(1−π0)​ℙ​(D=1∣F=1).\begin{split}R_{\mathrm{out}}&\leq\mathbb{P}(Y_{\tau}=0\mid D=1,F=1)\\ &\quad+\Bigl(1-\mathbb{P}(Y_{\tau}=0\mid D=1,F=1)\Bigr)\frac{\pi_{0}\alpha}{\pi_{0}\alpha+(1-\pi_{0})\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=1)}.\end{split}

Fix T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N}. Throughout the proof, probabilities and expectations are taken under the conditional law given F=0F=0. For readability, write ℙ0(⋅):=ℙ(⋅∣F=0)\mathbb{P}_{0}(\cdot):=\mathbb{P}(\cdot\mid F=0) and 𝔼0(⋅):=𝔼(⋅∣F=0)\mathbb{E}_{0}(\cdot):=\mathbb{E}(\cdot\mid F=0).

τnaive=inf{s≥1:ps≤α},\tau_{\mathrm{naive}}=\inf\{s\geq 1:p_{s}\leq\alpha\},

the event {τnaive>t}\{\tau_{\mathrm{naive}}>t\} is exactly the event that no crossing has occurred through time tt. Hence

At=⋂s=1t{ps>α}.A_{t}=\bigcap_{s=1}^{t}\{p_{s}>\alpha\}.

In particular, At∈𝒢tA_{t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}, and At−1∈𝒢t−1A_{t-1}\in\mathcal{G}_{t-1} for every t≥1t\geq 1. Also,

At=At−1∩{pt>α}.A_{t}=A_{t-1}\cap\{p_{t}>\alpha\}.

Step 2. Derive a one-step survival recursion. The assumption gives, for every t≥1t\geq 1,

ℙ⁡(pt≤α∣𝒢t−1,F=0)≥ctalmost surely.\mathbb{P}(p_{t}\leq\alpha\mid\mathcal{G}_{t-1},F=0)\geq c_{t}\qquad\text{almost surely}.

Since {pt>α}\{p_{t}>\alpha\} is the complement of {pt≤α}\{p_{t}\leq\alpha\},

ℙ⁡(pt>α∣𝒢t−1,F=0)=1−ℙ⁡(pt≤α∣𝒢t−1,F=0)≤1−ct.\mathbb{P}(p_{t}>\alpha\mid\mathcal{G}_{t-1},F=0)=1-\mathbb{P}(p_{t}\leq\alpha\mid\mathcal{G}_{t-1},F=0)\leq 1-c_{t}.

Now use At=At−1∩{pt>α}A_{t}=A_{t-1}\cap\{p_{t}>\alpha\}. We have

ℙ0(At)=𝔼0[𝟏{At}]=𝔼0[𝟏{At−1}𝟏{pt>α}].\mathbb{P}_{0}(A_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{0}\!\left[\mathbf{1}\{A_{t}\}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{0}\!\left[\mathbf{1}\{A_{t-1}\}\mathbf{1}\{p_{t}>\alpha\}\right].

Taking conditional expectation given 𝒢t−1\mathcal{G}_{t-1},

𝔼0[𝟏{At−1}𝟏{pt>α}]=𝔼0[𝔼0{𝟏{At−1}𝟏{pt>α}|𝒢t−1}].\mathbb{E}_{0}\!\left[\mathbf{1}\{A_{t-1}\}\mathbf{1}\{p_{t}>\alpha\}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{0}\!\left[\mathbb{E}_{0}\!\left\{\mathbf{1}\{A_{t-1}\}\mathbf{1}\{p_{t}>\alpha\}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{G}_{t-1}\right\}\right].

Because At−1∈𝒢t−1A_{t-1}\in\mathcal{G}_{t-1}, the indicator 𝟏​{At−1}\mathbf{1}\{A_{t-1}\} is 𝒢t−1\mathcal{G}_{t-1}-measurable, so

𝔼0{𝟏{At−1}𝟏{pt>α}|𝒢t−1}=𝟏{At−1}𝔼0[𝟏{pt>α}|𝒢t−1].\mathbb{E}_{0}\!\left\{\mathbf{1}\{A_{t-1}\}\mathbf{1}\{p_{t}>\alpha\}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{G}_{t-1}\right\}=\mathbf{1}\{A_{t-1}\}\mathbb{E}_{0}\!\left[\mathbf{1}\{p_{t}>\alpha\}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{G}_{t-1}\right].

𝔼0[𝟏{pt>α}|𝒢t−1]=ℙ(pt>α∣𝒢t−1,F=0).\mathbb{E}_{0}\!\left[\mathbf{1}\{p_{t}>\alpha\}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{G}_{t-1}\right]=\mathbb{P}(p_{t}>\alpha\mid\mathcal{G}_{t-1},F=0).

ℙ0​(At)=𝔼0​[𝟏​{At−1}​ℙ​(pt>α∣𝒢t−1,F=0)].\mathbb{P}_{0}(A_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{0}\!\left[\mathbf{1}\{A_{t-1}\}\mathbb{P}(p_{t}>\alpha\mid\mathcal{G}_{t-1},F=0)\right].

ℙ0​(AT)≤∏t=1T(1−ct).\mathbb{P}_{0}(A_{T})\leq\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1-c_{t}).

Because AT={τnaive>T}A_{T}=\{\tau_{\mathrm{naive}}>T\},

C.3 Proof of Theorem 1

Fix t≥1t\geq 1. By the countability of ℚ\mathbb{Q}, we may work on a full-probability event on which Assumption 1 holds simultaneously for every rational threshold q∈ℚq\in\mathbb{Q}. Thus, on this event, for every q∈ℚq\in\mathbb{Q},

ℙ(St≥q|𝒢~t−1,F=0)≤1n∑i=1n𝟏{Ri≥q}.\mathbb{P}\!\left(S_{t}\geq q\,\middle|\,\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=0\right)\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{R_{i}\geq q\}.

Fix a realization of 𝒢~t−1\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1} on this event and work under the corresponding conditional law given F=0F=0. Under this conditional law, the reference scores R1,…,RnR_{1},\ldots,R_{n} are fixed numbers. Let N(s):=∑i=1n𝟏{Ri≥s}N(s):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{R_{i}\geq s\}, so that pt=(1+N⁡(St))/(n+1)p_{t}=(1+N(S_{t}))/(n+1). Let R(1)≥R(2)≥⋯≥R(n)R_{(1)}\geq R_{(2)}\geq\cdots\geq R_{(n)} denote the reference scores sorted in non-increasing order, with ties kept with their multiplicities.

We prove that, for an arbitrary u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1],

ℙ(pt≤u|𝒢~t−1,F=0)≤u.\mathbb{P}\!\left(p_{t}\leq u\,\middle|\,\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=0\right)\leq u.

Step 1. Trivial endpoint cases. If u<1/(n+1)u<1/(n+1), then pt≥1/(n+1)p_{t}\geq 1/(n+1) almost surely, and hence

ℙ(pt≤u|𝒢~t−1,F=0)=0≤u.\mathbb{P}\!\left(p_{t}\leq u\,\middle|\,\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=0\right)=0\leq u.

If u=1u=1, the claim is immediate. It remains to consider u∈[1/(n+1),1)u\in[1/(n+1),1). Set k:=⌊(n+1)​u−1⌋k:=\lfloor(n+1)u-1\rfloor. Then k∈{0,1,…,n−1}k\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}.

Step 2. Reducing the small-pp event to an order-statistic tail event. On the event {pt≤u}\{p_{t}\leq u\}, we have

1+N⁡(St)n+1≤u.\frac{1+N(S_{t})}{n+1}\leq u.

Equivalently, 1+N⁡(St)≤(n+1)​u1+N(S_{t})\leq(n+1)u, so N⁡(St)≤(n+1)​u−1N(S_{t})\leq(n+1)u-1. Since N⁡(St)N(S_{t}) is integer-valued and k=⌊(n+1)​u−1⌋k=\lfloor(n+1)u-1\rfloor, this implies N⁡(St)≤kN(S_{t})\leq k.

We now show that N⁡(St)≤kN(S_{t})\leq k forces St>R(k+1)S_{t}>R_{(k+1)}. Suppose instead that St≤R(k+1)S_{t}\leq R_{(k+1)}. Then the k+1k+1 reference scores R(1),…,R(k+1)R_{(1)},\ldots,R_{(k+1)} are all at least StS_{t}. Hence N⁡(St)≥k+1N(S_{t})\geq k+1, contradicting N⁡(St)≤kN(S_{t})\leq k. Therefore,

{pt≤u}⊆{St>R(k+1)}.\{p_{t}\leq u\}\subseteq\{S_{t}>R_{(k+1)}\}.

Step 3. Applying dominance through rational thresholds. Let a:=R(k+1)a:=R_{(k+1)}. Choose a sequence of rational numbers qm↓aq_{m}\downarrow a with qm>aq_{m}>a for every mm. Since qm>a=R(k+1)q_{m}>a=R_{(k+1)}, at most kk reference scores are at least qmq_{m}. Thus N⁡(qm)≤kN(q_{m})\leq k. Applying Assumption 1 to the rational threshold qmq_{m} gives

ℙ(St≥qm|𝒢~t−1,F=0)≤N⁡(qm)n≤kn.\mathbb{P}\!\left(S_{t}\geq q_{m}\,\middle|\,\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=0\right)\leq\frac{N(q_{m})}{n}\leq\frac{k}{n}.

As m→∞m\to\infty, the events {St≥qm}\{S_{t}\geq q_{m}\} increase to {St>a}\{S_{t}>a\}. By continuity from below,

ℙ(St>a|𝒢~t−1,F=0)=limm→∞ℙ(St≥qm|𝒢~t−1,F=0)≤kn.\mathbb{P}\!\left(S_{t}>a\,\middle|\,\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=0\right)=\lim_{m\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\!\left(S_{t}\geq q_{m}\,\middle|\,\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=0\right)\leq\frac{k}{n}.

Step 4. Completing the super-uniformity bound. From Step 2, {pt≤u}⊆{St>a}\{p_{t}\leq u\}\subseteq\{S_{t}>a\}. Combining this inclusion with Step 3 gives

ℙ(pt≤u|𝒢~t−1,F=0)≤kn.\mathbb{P}\!\left(p_{t}\leq u\,\middle|\,\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=0\right)\leq\frac{k}{n}.

Since k=⌊(n+1)​u−1⌋k=\lfloor(n+1)u-1\rfloor, we have k≤(n+1)​u−1k\leq(n+1)u-1. Therefore,

kn≤(n+1)​u−1n=u+u−1n.\frac{k}{n}\leq\frac{(n+1)u-1}{n}=u+\frac{u-1}{n}.

Because u<1u<1 in the remaining case, (u−1)/n≤0(u-1)/n\leq 0, and hence

kn≤u.\frac{k}{n}\leq u.

Thus

ℙ(pt≤u|𝒢~t−1,F=0)≤u.\mathbb{P}\!\left(p_{t}\leq u\,\middle|\,\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t-1},F=0\right)\leq u.

Together with the endpoint cases in Step 1, this proves the desired inequality for every u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1]. Since the argument is pointwise on a full-probability event, the conditional super-uniformity statement holds almost surely. This proves (9). ∎

C.4 Proof of Proposition 3

Fix t≥1t\geq 1, and write ℋt:=𝒢~t\mathcal{H}_{t}:=\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t}. Throughout the proof, probabilities and expectations are taken under the conditional law given F=0F=0. We work on a full-probability event on which the conditional super-uniformity condition (9) holds for all u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1]. This is without loss, since it is enough to take the countable event on which (9) holds for all rational uu, and then extend to all uu by monotonicity and right-continuity of distribution functions.

Step 1. Reduce the e-process condition to a one-step p-to-e bound. Since

Et=Et−1​ft​(pt),E_{t}=E_{t-1}f_{t}(p_{t}),

and Et−1E_{t-1} is ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1}-measurable, we have

𝔼⁡(Et∣ℋt−1,F=0)=Et−1​𝔼​(ft​(pt)∣ℋt−1,F=0).\mathbb{E}(E_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0)=E_{t-1}\,\mathbb{E}(f_{t}(p_{t})\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0).

Thus it is enough to show that

𝔼⁡(ft​(pt)∣ℋt−1,F=0)≤1.\mathbb{E}(f_{t}(p_{t})\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0)\leq 1.

Conditional on ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1}, the predictable function ftf_{t} is fixed. Set g:=ftg:=f_{t}. Then g:[0,1]→[0,∞)g:[0,1]\to[0,\infty) is deterministic, non-increasing, and satisfies

∫01g⁡(u)​𝑑u=∫01ft​(u)​𝑑u≤1.\int_{0}^{1}g(u)\,du=\int_{0}^{1}f_{t}(u)\,du\leq 1.

Step 2. Convert monotonicity of gg into a lower-tail event for ptp_{t}. For each y≥0y\geq 0, define

Ay:={u∈[0,1]:g⁡(u)>y},ay:=λ⁡(Ay),A_{y}:=\{u\in[0,1]:g(u)>y\},\qquad a_{y}:=\lambda(A_{y}),

where λ\lambda denotes Lebesgue measure on [0,1][0,1]. Since gg is non-increasing, AyA_{y} is an initial segment of [0,1][0,1] in the following sense: if u∈Ayu\in A_{y} and 0≤v≤u0\leq v\leq u, then v∈Ayv\in A_{y}. Indeed, v≤uv\leq u implies g⁡(v)≥g⁡(u)>yg(v)\geq g(u)>y.

This implies that every u∈Ayu\in A_{y} satisfies u≤ayu\leq a_{y}. To see this, suppose u∈Ayu\in A_{y} and u>ayu>a_{y}. Since AyA_{y} contains the whole interval [0,u][0,u], its Lebesgue measure is at least uu, contradicting ay=λ⁡(Ay)<ua_{y}=\lambda(A_{y})<u. Therefore,

{g(pt)>y}={pt∈Ay}⊆{pt≤ay}.\{g(p_{t})>y\}=\{p_{t}\in A_{y}\}\subseteq\{p_{t}\leq a_{y}\}.

Step 3. Use conditional super-uniformity. By the inclusion from Step 2,

ℙ⁡(g⁡(pt)>y∣ℋt−1,F=0)≤ℙ⁡(pt≤ay∣ℋt−1,F=0).\mathbb{P}(g(p_{t})>y\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0)\leq\mathbb{P}(p_{t}\leq a_{y}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0).

Since ay∈[0,1]a_{y}\in[0,1], the conditional super-uniformity condition (9) gives

ℙ⁡(pt≤ay∣ℋt−1,F=0)≤ay.\mathbb{P}(p_{t}\leq a_{y}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0)\leq a_{y}.

Combining the last two displays,

ℙ⁡(g⁡(pt)>y∣ℋt−1,F=0)≤ay.\mathbb{P}(g(p_{t})>y\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0)\leq a_{y}.

Step 4. Integrate the tail bound. By the layer-cake identity for nonnegative random variables,

𝔼⁡(g⁡(pt)∣ℋt−1,F=0)=∫0∞ℙ⁡(g⁡(pt)>y∣ℋt−1,F=0)​𝑑y.\mathbb{E}(g(p_{t})\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}(g(p_{t})>y\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0)\,dy.

Using the bound from Step 3,

𝔼⁡(g⁡(pt)∣ℋt−1,F=0)≤∫0∞ay​𝑑y.\mathbb{E}(g(p_{t})\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0)\leq\int_{0}^{\infty}a_{y}\,dy.

Now substitute the definition ay=λ⁡(Ay)a_{y}=\lambda(A_{y}):

∫0∞ay​𝑑y=∫0∞λ⁡{u∈[0,1]:g⁡(u)>y}​𝑑y.\int_{0}^{\infty}a_{y}\,dy=\int_{0}^{\infty}\lambda\{u\in[0,1]:g(u)>y\}\,dy.

Writing the Lebesgue measure as an integral,

λ{u∈[0,1]:g(u)>y}=∫01𝟏{g(u)>y}du.\lambda\{u\in[0,1]:g(u)>y\}=\int_{0}^{1}\mathbf{1}\{g(u)>y\}\,du.

Substituting this into the preceding display gives

∫0∞aydy=∫0∞∫01𝟏{g(u)>y}dudy.\int_{0}^{\infty}a_{y}\,dy=\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{1}\mathbf{1}\{g(u)>y\}\,du\,dy.

Since the integrand is nonnegative, Tonelli’s theorem allows us to switch the order of integration:

∫0∞∫01𝟏{g(u)>y}dudy=∫01∫0∞𝟏{g(u)>y}dydu.\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{1}\mathbf{1}\{g(u)>y\}\,du\,dy=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbf{1}\{g(u)>y\}\,dy\,du.

For each fixed uu, the inner integral is

∫0∞𝟏{g(u)>y}dy=g(u),\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbf{1}\{g(u)>y\}\,dy=g(u),

because the indicator equals one exactly for 0≤y<g⁡(u)0\leq y<g(u). Therefore,

∫0∞ay​𝑑y=∫01g⁡(u)​𝑑u.\int_{0}^{\infty}a_{y}\,dy=\int_{0}^{1}g(u)\,du.

By Step 1, ∫01g⁡(u)​𝑑u≤1\int_{0}^{1}g(u)\,du\leq 1. Hence

𝔼⁡(g⁡(pt)∣ℋt−1,F=0)≤1.\mathbb{E}(g(p_{t})\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0)\leq 1.

Since g=ftg=f_{t}, this is

𝔼⁡(ft​(pt)∣ℋt−1,F=0)≤1.\mathbb{E}(f_{t}(p_{t})\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0)\leq 1.

Step 5. Complete the e-process verification. Returning to Et=Et−1​ft​(pt)E_{t}=E_{t-1}f_{t}(p_{t}), Step 1 and Step 4 give

𝔼⁡(Et∣ℋt−1,F=0)=Et−1​𝔼​(ft​(pt)∣ℋt−1,F=0)≤Et−1.\mathbb{E}(E_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0)=E_{t-1}\,\mathbb{E}(f_{t}(p_{t})\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0)\leq E_{t-1}.

Thus (Et)t≥0(E_{t})_{t\geq 0} is a nonnegative supermartingale under the infeasible regime F=0F=0, with E0=1E_{0}=1. Equivalently, it is an e-process for the infeasible regime. This proves Proposition 3. ∎

C.5 Proof of Proposition 4

Write ℙ0(⋅):=ℙ(⋅∣F=0)\mathbb{P}_{0}(\cdot):=\mathbb{P}(\cdot\mid F=0). By Proposition 3, (Et)t≥0(E_{t})_{t\geq 0} is a nonnegative supermartingale under ℙ0\mathbb{P}_{0}, with E0=1E_{0}=1.

Step 1. Relate terminal release to threshold crossing. Recall that τα:=inf{t≥1:Et≥1/α}\tau_{\alpha}:=\inf\{t\geq 1:E_{t}\geq 1/\alpha\} and D:=𝟏{τα≤Tmax}D:=\mathbf{1}\{\tau_{\alpha}\leq T_{\max}\}. Therefore,

{D=1}={τα≤Tmax}.\{D=1\}=\{\tau_{\alpha}\leq T_{\max}\}.

Since {τα≤Tmax}⊆{τα<∞}\{\tau_{\alpha}\leq T_{\max}\}\subseteq\{\tau_{\alpha}<\infty\}, we have

ℙ0​(D=1)≤ℙ0​(τα<∞).\mathbb{P}_{0}(D=1)\leq\mathbb{P}_{0}(\tau_{\alpha}<\infty).

Step 2. Express threshold crossing as a running supremum event. By definition of τα\tau_{\alpha}, the event {τα<∞}\{\tau_{\alpha}<\infty\} occurs exactly when the evidence process crosses 1/α1/\alpha at some finite time. Hence

{τα<∞}={supt≥1Et≥1α}.\{\tau_{\alpha}<\infty\}=\left\{\sup_{t\geq 1}E_{t}\geq\frac{1}{\alpha}\right\}.

Thus

ℙ0​(τα<∞)=ℙ0​(supt≥1Et≥1α).\mathbb{P}_{0}(\tau_{\alpha}<\infty)=\mathbb{P}_{0}\!\left(\sup_{t\geq 1}E_{t}\geq\frac{1}{\alpha}\right).

Step 3. Apply Ville’s inequality. Since (Et)t≥0(E_{t})_{t\geq 0} is a nonnegative supermartingale under ℙ0\mathbb{P}_{0} with E0=1E_{0}=1, Ville’s inequality gives

ℙ0​(supt≥1Et≥1α)≤α​E0=α.\mathbb{P}_{0}\!\left(\sup_{t\geq 1}E_{t}\geq\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)\leq\alpha E_{0}=\alpha.

Combining Steps 1–3,

ℙ⁡(D=1∣F=0)=ℙ0​(D=1)≤ℙ0​(τα<∞)≤α.\mathbb{P}(D=1\mid F=0)=\mathbb{P}_{0}(D=1)\leq\mathbb{P}_{0}(\tau_{\alpha}<\infty)\leq\alpha.

This proves Proposition 4. ∎

C.6 Proof of Proposition 5

Let OT=(ℛ,HT)O_{T}=(\mathcal{R},H_{T}), and let (𝖮T,𝒜T)(\mathsf{O}_{T},\mathcal{A}_{T}) denote the measurable space in which OTO_{T} takes values. Since DTD_{T} is measurable with respect to σ⁡(ℛ,HT)=σ⁡(OT)\sigma(\mathcal{R},H_{T})=\sigma(O_{T}), there exists a measurable map dT:𝖮T→{0,1}d_{T}:\mathsf{O}_{T}\to\{0,1\} such that DT=dT​(OT)D_{T}=d_{T}(O_{T}) almost surely. Define

A:={o∈𝖮T:dT​(o)=1}.A:=\{o\in\mathsf{O}_{T}:d_{T}(o)=1\}.

Then A∈𝒜TA\in\mathcal{A}_{T}.

Step 1. Express release probabilities as probabilities of the same event. For f∈{0,1}f\in\{0,1\}, the conditional law of OTO_{T} given F=fF=f is PfTP_{f}^{T}. Therefore,

ℙ⁡(DT=1∣F=f)=ℙ⁡(dT​(OT)=1∣F=f)=ℙ⁡(OT∈A∣F=f)=PfT​(A).\mathbb{P}(D_{T}=1\mid F=f)=\mathbb{P}(d_{T}(O_{T})=1\mid F=f)=\mathbb{P}(O_{T}\in A\mid F=f)=P_{f}^{T}(A).

In particular,

{ℙ⁡(DT=1∣F=1)=P1T​(A),ℙ⁡(DT=1∣F=0)=P0T​(A).\left\{\begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(D_{T}=1\mid F=1)&=P_{1}^{T}(A),\\ \mathbb{P}(D_{T}=1\mid F=0)&=P_{0}^{T}(A).\end{aligned}\right.

Step 2. Apply total variation to the release set. By the definition of total variation distance used here,

TV⁡(P1T,P0T)=supB∈𝒜T|P1T​(B)−P0T​(B)|.\TV(P_{1}^{T},P_{0}^{T})=\sup_{B\in\mathcal{A}_{T}}\left|P_{1}^{T}(B)-P_{0}^{T}(B)\right|.

Since A∈𝒜TA\in\mathcal{A}_{T}, taking B=AB=A in the supremum gives

|P1T​(A)−P0T​(A)|≤TV⁡(P1T,P0T).\left|P_{1}^{T}(A)-P_{0}^{T}(A)\right|\leq\TV(P_{1}^{T},P_{0}^{T}).

Also,

P1T​(A)−P0T​(A)≤|P1T​(A)−P0T​(A)|.P_{1}^{T}(A)-P_{0}^{T}(A)\leq\left|P_{1}^{T}(A)-P_{0}^{T}(A)\right|.

Combining the last two displays,

P1T​(A)−P0T​(A)≤TV⁡(P1T,P0T).P_{1}^{T}(A)-P_{0}^{T}(A)\leq\TV(P_{1}^{T},P_{0}^{T}).

Adding P0T​(A)P_{0}^{T}(A) to both sides yields

P1T​(A)≤P0T​(A)+TV⁡(P1T,P0T).P_{1}^{T}(A)\leq P_{0}^{T}(A)+\TV(P_{1}^{T},P_{0}^{T}).

Step 3. Translate back to release probabilities. Using the identities from Step 1,

{P1T​(A)=ℙ⁡(DT=1∣F=1),P0T​(A)=ℙ⁡(DT=1∣F=0).\left\{\begin{aligned} P_{1}^{T}(A)&=\mathbb{P}(D_{T}=1\mid F=1),\\ P_{0}^{T}(A)&=\mathbb{P}(D_{T}=1\mid F=0).\end{aligned}\right.

Substituting these identities into the bound from Step 2 gives

ℙ⁡(DT=1∣F=1)≤ℙ⁡(DT=1∣F=0)+TV⁡(P1T,P0T).\mathbb{P}(D_{T}=1\mid F=1)\leq\mathbb{P}(D_{T}=1\mid F=0)+\TV(P_{1}^{T},P_{0}^{T}).

This proves Proposition 5. ∎

C.7 Proof of Theorem 2

Write ℙ1(⋅):=ℙ(⋅∣F=1)\mathbb{P}_{1}(\cdot):=\mathbb{P}(\cdot\mid F=1), 𝔼1(⋅):=𝔼(⋅∣F=1)\mathbb{E}_{1}(\cdot):=\mathbb{E}(\cdot\mid F=1), and ℋt:=𝒢~t\mathcal{H}_{t}:=\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{t}. All probabilities and expectations below are taken under ℙ1\mathbb{P}_{1}.

Step 1. Relating terminal release to cumulative calibrated gain. Since pt∈[1/(n+1),1]p_{t}\in[1/(n+1),1] and ff is non-increasing, we have

f⁡(1/(n+1))≥f⁡(pt)≥f⁡(1)>0.f(1/(n+1))\geq f(p_{t})\geq f(1)>0.

Taking logarithms and subtracting log⁡f⁡(1)\log f(1) gives

log⁡ET=∑t=1T{log⁡f⁡(1)+Zt}=T​log⁡f⁡(1)+∑t=1TZt.\log E_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\{\log f(1)+Z_{t}\}=T\log f(1)+\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}.

Thus ET≥1/αE_{T}\geq 1/\alpha is equivalent to

T​log⁡f⁡(1)+∑t=1TZt≥log⁡(1/α),T\log f(1)+\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}\geq\log(1/\alpha),

which is equivalent, after subtracting T​log⁡f​(1)T\log f(1), to

∑t=1TZt≥log⁡(1/α)−T​log⁡f⁡(1)=Aα,T.\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}\geq\log(1/\alpha)-T\log f(1)=A_{\alpha,T}.

Therefore

{ET≥1/α}={∑t=1TZt≥Aα,T}.\{E_{T}\geq 1/\alpha\}=\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}\geq A_{\alpha,T}\right\}.

If ET≥1/αE_{T}\geq 1/\alpha, then the evidence process has crossed the release threshold by time TT, possibly first crossing exactly at TT. Hence

{∑t=1TZt≥Aα,T}⊆{τα≤T}.\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}\geq A_{\alpha,T}\right\}\subseteq\{\tau_{\alpha}\leq T\}.

Taking complements gives

{τα>T}⊆{∑t=1TZt<Aα,T},\{\tau_{\alpha}>T\}\subseteq\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}<A_{\alpha,T}\right\},

and therefore

ℙ1​(τα>T)≤ℙ1​(∑t=1TZt<Aα,T).\mathbb{P}_{1}(\tau_{\alpha}>T)\leq\mathbb{P}_{1}\!\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}<A_{\alpha,T}\right).

Step 2. From correct-candidate gain to a lower bound on expected total gain. Let mt:=𝔼1​(Zt∣ℋt−1)m_{t}:=\mathbb{E}_{1}(Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}). Also, since Yt∈{0,1}Y_{t}\in\{0,1\} and Zt≥0Z_{t}\geq 0, we have 0≤Yt​Zt≤Zt0\leq Y_{t}Z_{t}\leq Z_{t}. Taking conditional expectations given ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1} gives

∑t=1T𝔼1​(Yt​Zt∣ℋt−1)≤∑t=1Tmt.\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{1}(Y_{t}Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1})\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}m_{t}.

∑t=1T𝔼1​(Yt​Zt∣ℋt−1)≥BTalmost surely.\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{1}(Y_{t}Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1})\geq B_{T}\qquad\text{almost surely}.

C.8 Proof of Theorem 3

Fix T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N}. Throughout the proof, we work under the conditional law given σ⁡(ℛ)\sigma(\mathcal{R}) and on the event {F=0}\{F=0\}. Step 1. One-step inflation bound. Since et=f⁡(pt)e_{t}=f(p_{t}) and Qt,0=ℒ⁡(pt∣ℋt−1,F=0)Q_{t,0}=\mathcal{L}(p_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},F=0),

∫01g(u)Q(du)=∫0MQ{g>r}dr\int_{0}^{1}g(u)\,Q(du)=\int_{0}^{M}Q\{g>r\}\,dr

and

∫01g(u)P0(du)=∫0MP0{g>r}dr.\int_{0}^{1}g(u)\,P_{0}(du)=\int_{0}^{M}P_{0}\{g>r\}\,dr.

Subtracting the second display from the first gives

∫01g(u)Q(du)−∫01g(u)P0(du)=∫0M[Q{g>r}−P0{g>r}]dr.\int_{0}^{1}g(u)\,Q(du)-\int_{0}^{1}g(u)\,P_{0}(du)=\int_{0}^{M}\bigl[Q\{g>r\}-P_{0}\{g>r\}\bigr]\,dr.

For each rr, the set {u:g⁡(u)>r}\{u:g(u)>r\} is measurable, so

Q{g>r}−P0{g>r}≤TV(Q,P0).Q\{g>r\}-P_{0}\{g>r\}\leq\TV(Q,P_{0}).

Therefore,

∫01g⁡(u)​Q​(𝑑u)−∫01g⁡(u)​P0​(𝑑u)≤∫0MTV⁡(Q,P0)​dr.\int_{0}^{1}g(u)\,Q(du)-\int_{0}^{1}g(u)\,P_{0}(du)\leq\int_{0}^{M}\TV(Q,P_{0})\,dr.

Since TV⁡(Q,P0)\TV(Q,P_{0}) does not depend on rr,

∫0MTV⁡(Q,P0)​dr=M​TV⁡(Q,P0).\int_{0}^{M}\TV(Q,P_{0})\,dr=M\TV(Q,P_{0}).

Hence

∫01g⁡(u)​Q​(𝑑u)≤∫01g⁡(u)​P0​(𝑑u)+M​TV⁡(Q,P0).\int_{0}^{1}g(u)\,Q(du)\leq\int_{0}^{1}g(u)\,P_{0}(du)+M\TV(Q,P_{0}).

Applying this inequality with g=fg=f and Q=Qt,0Q=Q_{t,0}, we obtain

∫01f⁡(u)​Qt,0​(𝑑u)≤∫01f⁡(u)​P0​(𝑑u)+M​TV⁡(Qt,0,P0).\int_{0}^{1}f(u)\,Q_{t,0}(du)\leq\int_{0}^{1}f(u)\,P_{0}(du)+M\TV(Q_{t,0},P_{0}).

By the theorem assumptions, ∫01f⁡(u)​P0​(𝑑u)≤1\int_{0}^{1}f(u)\,P_{0}(du)\leq 1 and TV⁡(Qt,0,P0)≤ϵ\TV(Q_{t,0},P_{0})\leq\epsilon. Substituting these two bounds gives

∫01f⁡(u)​Qt,0​(𝑑u)≤1+M​ϵ.\int_{0}^{1}f(u)\,Q_{t,0}(du)\leq 1+M\epsilon.

Since β=1+M​ϵ\beta=1+M\epsilon, we conclude that

𝔼ℛ,0​(et∣ℋt−1)≤β.\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{R},0}(e_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1})\leq\beta.

Since ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0 and M≥0M\geq 0, we have β=1+M​ϵ≥1\beta=1+M\epsilon\geq 1. Because t≤Tt\leq T and β≥1\beta\geq 1,

{τα≤T}⊆{sup1≤t≤TE~t≥β−Tα−1}.\{\tau_{\alpha}\leq T\}\subseteq\left\{\sup_{1\leq t\leq T}\widetilde{E}_{t}\geq\beta^{-T}\alpha^{-1}\right\}.

ℙℛ,0​(sup1≤t≤TE~t≥β−T​α−1)≤𝔼ℛ,0​(E~0)β−T​α−1.\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{R},0}\!\left(\sup_{1\leq t\leq T}\widetilde{E}_{t}\geq\beta^{-T}\alpha^{-1}\right)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{R},0}(\widetilde{E}_{0})}{\beta^{-T}\alpha^{-1}}.

Since E~0=1\widetilde{E}_{0}=1,

𝔼ℛ,0​(E~0)β−T​α−1=1β−T​α−1.\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{R},0}(\widetilde{E}_{0})}{\beta^{-T}\alpha^{-1}}=\frac{1}{\beta^{-T}\alpha^{-1}}.

1β−T​α−1=βT​α.\frac{1}{\beta^{-T}\alpha^{-1}}=\beta^{T}\alpha.

α​βT=α​(1+M​ϵ)T.\alpha\beta^{T}=\alpha(1+M\epsilon)^{T}.

Hence

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
